Vanilla Bean Rooibos Ice Cream
1 cup Whole Milk (avoid ultra-pasteurized)
2 cups Heavy Cream (avoid ultra-pasteurized)
2 tablespoons Organic Rooibos Tea Leaves
1 Madigascar Vanilla Bean, split and seeds scraped
3 tablespoons Honey
6 Large Egg Yolks
1 tablespoon Amaretto Liquer
3/4 cup Chopped Raw Almonds
Dulce de Leche
1 quart Whole Milk (avoid ultra pasteurized)
1 cup Sugar
3 tablespoons Honey
1 Vanilla bean, split and seeds scraped
1/2 teaspoon baking soda
Place the milk, sugar, vanilla bean, and honey into a medium saucepan, over medium heat. Bring the mixture just to a simmer, stirring occasionally to dissolve the sugar, and remove from the heat. Add the rooibos tea leaves, cover, and steep for 1 hour (NOTE: the long steep is critical for the best flavor). Add one cup of the cream to the tea/milk base, and warm the mixture (do NOT boil). Strain to remove the rooibos leave and vanilla bean (but don't worry if there are a few leaves remaining (they will be strained again). Discard the rooibos leaves; rinse and retain the vanilla bean. Set aside the remaining one cup of heavy cream in a medium bowl with a strainer on top. In a medium mixing bowl whisk the egg yolks until they lighten in color. Gradually add the warm cream base to the eggs. Temper the cream mixture into the eggs by gradually adding small amounts, until the remainder is incorporated. Return the egg and cream mixture to the saucepan and place over low heat. Continue to cook, stirring frequently, until the mixture thickens slightly and coats the back of a spoon and reaches 170 to 175 degrees F. Strain the mixture into the one cup of cream previously set aside. Return the previously used vanilla bean to the mixture and place into an ice bath for 30 minutes. Place the mixture into the refrigerator for 4 to 8 hours or until the temperature reaches 40 degrees F or below. Remove the vanilla bean, pour the cooled cream mixture into an ice cream maker. Add one teaspoon of amaretto and process according to the manufacturer's directions. This should take approximately 25 to 35 minutes. In the last 5 minutes, add the raw almonds to incorporate (this step can be skipped if you don't care for nuts). Scoop the ice cream into a freezer proof container in sections, layering spoonfuls of the (refrigerated) Dulce De Leche between the layers, swirling to create a random pattern. Freeze for 3 to 4 hours to allow the ice cream to harden. Combine the milk, sugar, honey, vanilla bean and seeds in a large, 4-quart saucepan and place over medium heat. Bring to a simmer, stirring occasionally, until the sugar has dissolved. Once the sugar has dissolved, add the baking soda and stir to combine. Reduce the heat to low and cook uncovered at a bare simmer. Stir occasionally, but do not re-incorporate the foam that appears on the top of the mixture. Continue to cook for 1 hour. Remove the vanilla bean after 1 hour and continue to cook until the mixture is a dark caramel color and has reduced to about 1 cup, approximately 1 1/2 to 2 hours. Strain the mixture through a fine mesh strainer. Store in the refrigerator in a sealed container until thoroughly cooled.

More than 5.2 million Germans were out of work in February, new figures show.
The figure of 5.216 million people, or 12.6% of the working-age population, is the highest jobless rate in Europe's biggest economy since the 1930s. The news comes as the head of Germany's panel of government economic advisers predicted growth would again stagnate. Speaking on German TV, Bert Ruerup said the panel's earlier forecast of 1.4% was too optimistic and warned growth would be just 1% in 2005.
The German government is trying to tackle the stubbornly-high levels of joblessness with a range of labour market reforms. At their centre is the "Hartz-IV" programme introduced in January to shake up welfare benefits and push people back into work - even if some of the jobs are heavily subsidised. The latest unemployment figures look set to increase the pressure on the government. Widely leaked to the German newspapers a day in advance, they produced screaming headlines criticising Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder's Social Democrat-Green Party administration. Mr Schroeder had originally come into office promising to halve unemployment.
Still, some measures suggest the picture is not quite so bleak. The soaring official unemployment figure follows a change in the methodology which pushed up the jobless rate by more than 500,000 in January. Adjusted for seasonal changes, the overall unemployment rate is 4.875 million people or 11.7%, up 0.3 percentage points from the previous month. Using the most internationally-accepted methodology of the International Labour Organisation (ILO), Germany had 3.97 million people out of work in January. And ILO-based figures also suggest that 14,000 new net jobs were created that month, taking the number of people employed to 38.9 million. The ILO defines an unemployed person as someone who in the previous four weeks had actively looked for work they could take up immediately.

We propose Deep Neural Network (DNN)-based image analysis technique to segment raw RGB images taken of thin polished concrete samples under a digital optical microscope. Deep learning is gaining significant popularity in computer vision. We employ a state-of-the-art fully convolutional DNN (FCN) to extract semantic image segmentation of the microscopic RGB image. The network is trained on our custom-annotated concrete microscopy set (CS-Concrete Microscopy). Using the FCN-based semantic segmentation approach provides several key advantages in concrete petrographic image analysis. First, the resulting segmentation masks make it easier to interpret the images by automatically selecting the desired elements of interest and removing irrelevant information. Second, DNN-based segmentation enables precise measurement of petrographic image features and avoids the tedious process of manual human annotations that are highly susceptible to human subjectivity. To show the utility of our deep learning image analysis framework, we developed a quantitative segmentation evaluation metric, called Segmetric Index of Fidelity (SiF) for our CS-Concrete Microscopy. The segmentation metric is designed to evaluate the segmentation quality of the model on an unbiased test dataset. We found a correlation between the SiF score and the accuracy of automatic segmentation of microscopic image features. The automatic segmentation approach using SiF has the potential to significantly reduce time and effort of manual microscopic image analysis.
The paper is authored by a team of researchers/scientists from the Civil and Environmental Engineering Department at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, the Wisconsin Center for Advancing Research in Transportation, the Department of Engineering Professional Development, the Department of Civil Engineering at Pohang University of Science and Technology, and from Korea Research Institute of Standards and Science (KRISS).
While the research paper appears to suggest that deep learning-based image recognition/ segmentation is better (objective) and more reliable, it's unclear to me why one cannot just measure concrete with digital callipers. It doesn't look like these researchers did a comparative study of the various image segmentation techniques on a standard dataset containing different variations of the images in their dataset. But then again, the study wasn't meant to be a comparison and may have other benefits.
One could also argue that while deep learning-based image segmentation is objectively better, it is also more expensive as it requires expensive deep learning-based AI

In a large pot, combine 2 cups water and 3 cups low sodium chicken broth, bringing it to a simmer with 1 tsp salt. Ingredients:

- 4 large potatoes, peeled and cubed
- 1 large onion, chopped
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth
- 1 cup skim milk
- 1/2 cup low-fat sour cream
- 1/2 teaspoon salt
- 1/4 teaspoon black pepper
- 1/4 teaspoon paprika
- 2 tablespoons chopped fresh chives
- 1/2 cup shredded low-fat cheddar cheese

Instructions:

1. In a large pot, combine the potatoes, onion, garlic, and chicken broth. Bring to a boil over high heat.

2. Reduce the heat to medium-low and let it simmer until the potatoes are tender, about 15-20 minutes.

3. Use an immersion blender to puree the soup until smooth. If you don't have an immersion blender, you can transfer the soup to a regular blender in batches and puree it that way. Just be careful as the soup will be hot.

4. Return the soup to the pot (if you used a regular blender) and stir in the skim milk, low-fat sour cream, salt, pepper, and paprika. Heat the soup over medium heat until it's heated through.

5. Ladle the soup into bowls and top each serving with a sprinkle of chives and shredded low-fat cheddar cheese.

6. Serve the soup hot with a side of crusty bread if desired.

This Creamy Potato Soup is low in fat but high in flavor. It's the perfect comfort food for a cold day. Enjoy!

An upward trend is observable in the number of students residing south of the boundary submitting applications to Scottish universities. This surge, however, will not impede Scottish students from gaining admission. Between January 2005 and the preceding year, applications from England and Wales experienced a growth of 17%, with a total of 27,700 applicants. Concerns had previously arisen concerning a potential wave of "fee refugees" seeking refuge from top-up fees capping at £3,000 annually in England. Last June, Minister for Lifelong Learning Jim Wallace unveiled plans to boost tuition fees for English students studying in Scotland by £2,000 to deter a mass exodus; nevertheless, no definitive sum has been established. The legislation authorizing these top-up fees in England isn't set to materialize until autumn 2006, and pupils initiating their studies prior to this period won't encounter extra expenses whatsoever.

Ucas disclosed these statistics on Thursday. Universities Scotland, which advocates for university heads, maintained that this uptick in applications didn't signify Scottish students being marginalized. Director David Caldwell conveyed to BBC Radio Scotland's Good Morning Scotland program that some scholars might be attempting to evade prospective escalations in English universities' annual fees, though this wasn't a dominant motive. He added: "Scottish universities are esteemed for their exceptional caliber, captivating curricula, and Scotland's allure as a desirable location for learning. Students recognize that upon commencing their education in 2006, they will confront top-up fees if they enroll in an English university, and this could contribute to the heightened interest in Scottish institutions. However, it does not imply an influx of countless more English students studying here." Mr. Wallace concurred and emphasized that the data necessitated careful consideration. He clarified that the application surge should be assessed in relation to other factors.

Mixture for Crust and Topping:
Mix together 2 cups quick-cooking rolled oats, 1/4 tsp salt, 1.5 tsp baking powder, 1 cup lightly packed brown sugar, and 1.5 cups all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 1 cup margarine or butter and use a fork or pastry blender to create a crumbly texture. Set aside 50% of this mixture for the topping. Press the other half evenly into a 9x12 inch baking dish.

Filling:
In a separate bowl, whisk together 2 tbsp cornstarch and 1 cup white sugar. Blend in 1 beaten egg and continue mixing until smooth. Stir in 3 cups chopped fresh or frozen rhubarb and 1 cup drained canned pineapple. Add 1 tsp cinnamon and combine thoroughly. Pour filling over crust in the baking dish and sprinkle the reserved crumbly oat mixture on top.

Bake at 350°F (175°C) for approximately 45 to 50 minutes or until golden brown. Allow it to rest briefly prior to serving. Serve with your preferred ice-cream or whipped cream.

On May 11, 2012, the Ambedkar cartoon controversy caused disruption in the Indian Parliament, leading to the adjournment of both the Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha. Thirumavalavan, a Tamil Nadu MP, raised the matter in Lok Sabha but was initially barred from speaking about it. He subsequently displayed the contentious cartoon depicting Dr. B.R. Ambedkar being driven by Jawaharlal Nehru as if they were pulling a snail representing the Indian Constitution. This representation was perceived as disrespectful by the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The cartoon originated from a book published by NCERT in 2006, under the supervision of the Ministry of Human Resources during the tenure of the United Progressive Alliance (UPA) led by Sonia Gandhi (Indian National Congress). By Edna St. Vincent Millay

Among the many hundred thousand people of Paris,
There is one who is quite unusually fair,
And when I saw her for the first time I felt uneasy,
As though I knew not what to do or where to turn.

It was not her eyes, though they were sweet and mild;
It was not her mouth, though the lips were fresh and red:
It was not her cheeks, though they were soft and warm;
It was not even he breast, though it was beautiful and round.

It was her hair: oh, glorious, glossy stuff!
It gleamed and it shone, a rich golden brown,
The glory of Youth, the joy of Summer's day,
And my heart stopped, and I forgot to run.

And then I knew 'twas not her hair alone,
But all of her body, and her spirit as well,
That made me know I had never seen anyone
Who looked, or felt, or thought, as she did.

And so I loved her, though I knew it all along,
From the moment that I first set eyes on her sweet,
Dear face, and her lovely, perfect body,
I loved her, and every day I love her yet.

But what is the use of talking about love?
For Heaven knows, in this dull world Love's dreams are vain,
And so I shut my eyes and dream about her none,
But live and work, and pray for a better time.

And though there were a million other girls
Just as lovely as she is anywhere,
I know that in all the world there is only one
Who is exactly like she is, and that is she.

And when I die, I will surely go to her,
For Death could not come between us, were it tried,
And so I have no fear of dying suddenly,
For I shall only be going to her side.

Though she will not know it, unless God should will
That women here on earth should have a soul as men,
Still, when I reach the other side, and leave this world of sin,
I'll find her waiting, and tell her all.

About how much I love her, and learn from her lips
The story of her life, and what makes her so sweet:
I'll ask

Gordon Brown is to freeze petrol duty increases, fund a £1bn package to avoid big council tax rises and boost childcare and maternity leave.
In an upbeat pre-Budget report, he slightly increased borrowing but insisted economic targets would be met. The chancellor also hailed the longest period of growth in UK "industrial history" but denied he was "gloating". But Oliver Letwin, for the Tories, attacked government red tape and debt, dubbing Mr Brown "Sir Wastealot".
The shadow chancellor said Mr Brown's "golden rule" had "turned to dross in his hands" and said he was borrowing to spend, not invest, with predicted debt over the coming years totalling £170bn. Mr Letwin told MPs: "The tide is going out on the chancellor's credibility. He is spending, borrowing and taxing so much because he is not getting value for taxpayer's money."
Vincent Cable, for the Liberal Democrats, accused Mr Brown of ducking tough choices.
He said: "Last week the prime minister gave us the politics of fear; this week the chancellor has offered the economics of complacency. "There are serious challenges ahead from the falling dollar and from the rapid downturn in the UK housing market and rising personal debt. But they have not been confronted." Mr Brown rejected the Lib Dem's call to open up the government's books to the National Audit Office, saying decisions on tax and spending should be made by ministers. Some economists say his forecasts on public finances are wishful thinking. BBC economic editor Evan Davis said the figures were plausible but also a gamble.
Mr Brown's insistence he was not "gloating" was a pointed rebuttal of a warning from new European Commissioner Peter Mandelson. In his speech, he set out a 10-year childcare strategy for if Labour wins the next election.
It includes a £285m cash injection to extend paid maternity leave from six months to nine, with parents able to transfer leave from the mother to the father. He also promised to increase free nursery education for three and four-year-olds to 15 hours from April 2007. And funds would be provided to keep schools open from 0800 to 1800GMT to look after children while their parents were at work. Taken together, the measures would create a "welfare state that is truly family-friendly for the first time in its history", said Mr Brown. He also announced a cash hand-out for older pensioners, with payments of £50 for the over-70s as part of the winter fuel allowance. In a move ministers say should keep council tax rises below 5% next year, the chancellor said he was providing an extra £1bn for local councils. The money is expected to come from government departments such as health and education.
Mr Brown said he was set to meet his two fiscal rules - to borrow only to invest and keep debt "low and sustainable" - both in this economic cycle and the next. Borrowing figures for 2003/4 are £35bn - £2.5bn less than the £37.5bn predicted in March's budget, as already announced by the Office for National Statistics. Borrowing is tipped to fall to £31bn by 2005/06 - but that is still £2bn more than Mr Brown predicted in his March budget. Inflation would be 1.75% next year and 2% in the years to follow, Mr Brown forecast. He also pledged an extra £105m for security and counter-terrorism. Business groups have welcomed efforts to improve competitiveness and invest more in skills and innovation. But there worries about the costs of more family-friendly working. Simon Sweetman, from the Federation of Small Businesses, said: "The proposals on maternity leave have clearly been made with a general election in mind and with little thought to the impact on small employers."

Here is the abstract for the academic paper titled "A 2D dilated residual U-Net for multi-organ segmentation in thoracic CT":

Abstract: We present a 2D dilated residual U-Net for multi-organ segmentation in thoracic CT scans. Our network is designed to address the challenges of segmenting multiple organs in thoracic CT, which often have complex shapes and overlapping structures. The key innovation in our network is the use of dilated convolutions, which enable the network to capture more context and details from the input images. We also introduce a residual connection module that facilitates the training process and improves the performance of the network. Our network is trained on a large dataset of thoracic CT scans and evaluated on the publicly available MICCAI 2017 Multi-Organ Segmentation Challenge dataset. We achieve competitive results on the challenge dataset and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in segmenting multiple organs in thoracic CT.

The sachem (sakim, sagamore, sagamo, sahe) was the chief or head among the indigenous people of New England. The title was used during the 17th and 18th centuries. According to the Oxford English Dictionary the word is a corruption "by folk etymology" of the phrase "by and by chief", in imitation of the Algonquian expression for it, meaning "Great Sachem" or "Head-Man-By-And-By" (cf. Byram).
The English word "sachem" derives from the earlier pronunciation "sagamore".
The title Sachem was typically used for the leaders of a given sachemdom or wampum belt. Wampum belts were similar to the Roman "tribute of nations" or Iroquois "league of nations", representing a confederacy of tribes. A sachemdom could comprise numerous individual (or autonomous or semi-autonomous?) bands, which could be identified by a local term. There was great fluidity among bands, so that at any given time one could identify many bands but any particular band might represent a different collection of tribes several decades hence.
Sachemdoms were ruled by a "Great Sachem". The Great Sachem was usually selected in a way similar to other forms of autocracy, sometimes through a trial by combat. In some places there was a council of sachems who advised the Great Sachem. However, it is not clear that the Great Sachem actually held sway over all the sachems (e.g. if he could override their decisions, etc.), but in general seemed to rule through consensus.
The Sachemship of Narragansett, for example, was established in 1643 and the first Great Sachem was Canonicus, son of Miantunnomu.
After the Great Sachem's death or retirement, his son often became successor. In some cases, when there was no clear heir, the Narragansett elected a Great Sachem. The last Great Sachem of the Narragansett, Joseph Jenks, was elected and ruled until 1858, when the Great Sachem was deposed, and the sachemship was abolished.

The UK Independence Party has lost one of its two London Assembly members to Robert Kilroy-Silk's new political party, expected to launch on Wednesday.
Damian Hockney said ex-chatshow host Mr Kilroy-Silk would "deliver better" as the leader of a eurosceptic party. He said Mr Kilroy-Silk had made him deputy party leader of Veritas, Latin for truth. Sources close to Mr Hockney said around eight other members of London UKIP were also planning to jump ship.
Details of the coming week's events were hammered out at a meeting at Mr Kilroy-Silk's Buckinghamshire home on Sunday, the BBC News Website was told. The news came after UKIP suspended a candidate for allegedly suggesting the criminally insane should be killed. John Houston, 54, was due to stand in the East Kilbride seat in Lanarkshire at the next election. A spokesman for UKIP called on Mr Hockney to quit the London Assembly. UKIP asserts that Mr Hockney "has a moral obligation, if not a legal one" to stand down. Mr Hockney meanwhile told the BBC: "I believe that Robert Kilroy-Silk can deliver better as a leader of a eurosceptic party than the current leadership of the UK Independence Party."
On the suspension of Mr Houston, UKIP said those who selected him knew nothing of his views. Mr Houston is alleged to have said that the organs of the criminally insane should be "made available to law-abiding members of the community" and proposed the legalisation of drugs and the sex trade.
The document reportedly said: "We're looking for the resurrection of the British Empire. "The problems for the human race - environmental and others - can only be dealt with on a global scale, and that calls for a radical alliance of the English-speaking nations, which they are uniquely able to do." UKIP spokesman Mark Croucher said the main issue would be that Mr Houston's reported views had been presented as UKIP policy, which they were not.

In the lengthy, narrow dwelling's hall, a faded photograph of me at four hangs: hand in hand with my bushy-browed grandpa, donning a plaid woolen cap and a sweater embellished with reindeer. This younger self gazes into the camera lens, smiling demurely, cheeks pale from a recent haircut, so pure as to border on naivete. Treading the fence of melancholy, I yearn to share some wisdom:

About life in Grampa's yard, in Rochester, New York, during the year of nineteen fifty-one, I'd caution that existence brings pain: fractured emotions, unforeseen mishaps, sirens wailing, beloved ones taken away, shabby, monochrome farewells, dreams crumbling. I'd murmur about an emptiness lurking: deep, vortexing, and dark enough to fracture spirits. I'd advise him to check traffic before crossing, and to bundle up against winter's chill. I'd implore him to be cautious. "Beware," I'd plead. "Take care..."

But he wouldn't listen.
He continues to smile.
(Unable to save him.)
Life had already claimed him.
A constant truth back then:
Rochester's yards,
Summertime's fireflies,
The year nineteen fifty-one.

Now, all that remains is this:
Somehow, I find myself cherishing that child.
I wish him to understand.
(Written 1984, Revised 2004)

Cole makes five central points. First, he states that Al-Qaeda is better thought of as a small cult rather than a true mass movement like fascism or communism in the early 20th century. Second, he states that the Muslim world contains large sections of people who can be potential allies to the U.S. Third, he states that American energy independence cannot really happen. Fourth, he states that Iran is not an implacable enemy of the U.S. and should be engaged with. Fifth, he states that coalition forces in Iraq should undergo a careful, deliberate military disengagement rather than an immediate withdrawal or an extended military presence. Other People's Money begins just before the 1987 stock market crash, and describes the conflict between a ruthless, predatory leveraged buyout specialist, Larry Crowne, and his longtime rival, Henry Ross, who is the CEO of a well-established family-owned bank. Crowne specializes in hostile takeovers of companies, buying them, and breaking them up for profit. In this instance, Crowne is attempting to buy United States Electrical, a lighting fixture company based in Providence, Rhode Island. Ross is convinced that UE is a solid company and will not break up the company, and he tries to rally the UE employees to fight off the takeover.

As the story progresses, Crowne's leveraged buyouts grow larger and more daring, and he becomes increasingly entangled with the political establishment, most notably with GovernorDX, who is running for the United States Senate. Crowne initially supports DX's campaign, but ends up supporting his opponent Jack Riley when DX takes a stance that favors organized labor, which would make it more difficult for Crowne to take over companies.

The novel traces Crowne's meteoric rise as he arranges ever-larger takeovers of major corporations, while Henry Ross tries in vain to rally the company owners whose businesses are being taken over. Meanwhile, DX's political career becomes increasingly entangled with Crowne's business dealings. In the end, Crowne's ambitions get the better of him when he attempts to buy a major New York bank, and instead ends up being wiped out when the stock market crash of 1987 occurs.

The story is of three sisters, of whom the youngest is chosen by Tsar Saltan (Saltán) to be his wife, while he makes the other two his royal cook and royal weaver. They are jealous, of course, and when the tsar goes off to war, and in his absence the tsaritsa gives birth to a son, Prince Gvidon (Gvidón), they arrange to have her and her child sealed up in a barrel and thrown into the sea. The sea itself takes pity on them, and they are cast up on the shore of a remote island, Buyan. The son, having quickly grown while in the barrel, goes hunting. He ends up saving an enchanted swan from a kite. The swan creates a city for Prince Gvidon to rule, but he is homesick, and the swan turns him into a mosquito. In this guise, he visits Tsar Saltan's court, where he stings his aunt in the eye and escapes. Back in his distant realm, the swan gives Gvidon a magical squirrel. But he continues to pine for home, so the swan transforms him into a fly. In this guise, Prince Gvidon visit's Saltan's court again and he stings his older aunt in the eye. The third time, the Prince is transformed into a bumblebee and stings the nose of his grandmother. In the end, he expresses a desire for a bride instead of his old home, at which point the swan is revealed to be a beautiful princess, whom he marries. He is visited by the Tsar, who is overjoyed to find his wife and newly-married son.

The Normalized Cut (NCut) objective function in data clustering and image segmentation assesses graph partitioning costs with a preference for evenly distributed clusters. This propensity results in exclusion of singleton partitions, even for loosely linked vertices. Inspired by the Bühler-Hein family of balanced cut costs, we introduce the Compassionately Conservative Balanced (CCB) Cut costs. These costs, adjustable via a parameter, offer a balance between minimizing numerous singleton partitions and maintaining equilibrium among all partitions. We prove that CCB-Cut optimization can be transformed into an orthogonally constrained $\ell_{\tau}$-minimization problem identical to Computing Piecewise Flat Embeddings (PFE) for a specific index. We develop an Irrational Rayleigh Quotient (IRRQ) algorithm to solve the relaxed problem iteratively. Our experiments using BSDS500 database images demonstrate improved accuracy and more diverse region sizes for CCB-Cut-based image segmentation compared to NCut-based methods.

Engineering firm Balfour Beatty and five railway managers are to go on trial for manslaughter over the Hatfield rail crash in 2000.
Four people died when a section of rail broke and a high speed train derailed. Balfour Beatty's railway maintenance arm was in charge of the upkeep of the line at Hatfield, Hertfordshire. Balfour Beatty managers Anthony Walker and Nicholas Jeffries, and Railtrack managers Alistair Cook, Sean Fugill and Keith Lea all face individual charges. All five men, along with four others, are also accused of breaches of health and safety laws. Balfour Beatty Rail Maintenance faces a corporate manslaughter charge. It is expected the trial could last as long as a year. The accident, on 17 October 2000, happened when the London to Leeds express came off the tracks at 115 mph, when it was derailed by a cracked section of rail. The accident on the East Coast Main Line sparked major disruption. The overall responsibility for the line was Railtrack's - the company that has now become Network Rail. Those who died in the accident were Steve Arthur, 46, from Pease Pottage, West Sussex; Peter Monkhouse, 50, of Headingley, Leeds; Leslie Gray, 43, of Tuxford, Nottingham; and Robert James Alcorn, 37, of Auckland, New Zealand.

Osteoarthritis (OA) represents a significant health concern for the elderly population. MRI is commonly used to assess and monitor OA progression, but its high analysis costs and susceptibility to human error and subjectivity limit its efficiency and accuracy. Computer-assisted knee MRI segmentation has gained increasing attention as it offers relief to medical professionals from labor-intensive tasks and enhances diagnostic precision, holding substantial promise for clinical practice and research. Over the last few decades, various automatic and semi-automatic techniques for knee MRI segmentation have been explored extensively. Yet, a comprehensive review on this topic remains absent. In this survey paper, we categorize existing methods based on underlying principles and examine their current research standing while suggesting potential avenues for future investigation.

In this paper, we present a state-of-the-art architecture for real-time person segmentation. Our method is fully automatic, requires no user input, and can be run on CPUs. We do so by training a single deep network that operates on RGB images of a whole person. Our network is trained to predict a confidence map that is used to obtain pixelwise human masks. Our main contribution is a novel loss function for training the network, composed of pixel-wise and group-wise losses. The group-wise loss explicitly penalizes segmentation errors on the boundary, leading to precise predictions in challenging situations, such as occlusions and self-occlusions. To achieve real-time performance, our network, dubbed keypoint transfer (KT), is based on keypoint detection and transfer, where segmentation masks are predicted for keypoint locations, and transferred to all pixels of the image. This step requires very few operations, compared to convolutions, and therefore is suitable for efficient inference on a CPU. We also use it to generate new training data, which is made compatible with the network through the use of a group-wise loss. KT provides state-of-the-art segmentation accuracy for multi-person scenarios, while also running at 30 frames per second on an unmodified CPU.

China's biggest spirits maker, Kweichow Moutai, has signed a deal to boost its presence in Italy's booming wine market by distributing its products through Illva Saronno, one of the country's oldest and biggest liquor companies.

The partnership, sealed on Thursday, gives Illva Saronno, producer of the Disaronno liqueur, distribution rights to Moutai's portfolio of baijiu, a distilled grain spirit usually made from sorghum.

Illva said in a statement that the partnership aimed to "strengthen the presence of both companies on their respective home markets and to develop business opportunities in third countries".

Moutai, whose fiery liquor is a favourite tipple of China's ruling Communist Party elite, has been looking to expand its global footprint.

The company's lustre has dimmed somewhat in China in recent months as its flagship baijiu product has fallen out of favour with some younger consumers, who have turned to imported spirits such as Scotch whisky.

However, it remains immensely popular in China, with its sales jumping 25% in the first half of 2022, and it is hoping to win over new consumers in Europe and elsewhere.

Chinese drinks companies have been looking to expand abroad as domestic consumption slows and foreign sales of Chinese spirits, wine and beer are growing quickly.

China's beer giant Budweiser Brewing Co Ltd, formed by the merger of Budweiser and local giant Tsingtao, has said it aims to become one of the world's top 10 beer companies within a decade.

In July, Budweiser Brewing signed a deal with Coca-Cola Co's Costa coffee chain to roll out a line of coffee-flavoured drinks in China.

The unemployment rate in Australia has reached its highest point in four years, according to recent data released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics. The jobless rate increased from 5.5% in December 2018 to 5.7% in January 2019, marking the first rise since August last year.

While this increase may be cause for concern, experts have noted that it is still within the range considered healthy for the economy. In addition, they pointed out that the participation rate - which measures the proportion of working-age people who are either employed or looking for work - remained steady at 65.6%, indicating that there was no significant drop in workforce engagement.

Furthermore, Prime Minister Scott Morrison hailed the figures as evidence that his government's economic policies were paying off. He emphasized that over 500,000 jobs had been created under his administration and vowed to continue supporting businesses and workers alike.

However, opposition leader Bill Shorten criticized the government's handling of the situation, arguing that inadequate investment in education and training was contributing to skill shortages and wage stagnation. He called on the government to do more to address these issues and ensure sustainable growth for all Australians.

Overall, while the latest employment numbers paint a mixed picture, they serve as a reminder that Australia's labour market remains resilient despite global uncertainties and domestic challenges.

We present a fully relativistic calculation of the observed galaxy number
counts in the linear regime. We show that besides the density fluctuations and
redshift-space distortions, various relativistic effects contribute to
observations at large scales. These effects all have the same physical origin:
they result from the fact that our coordinate system, namely the galaxy
redshift and the incoming photons' direction, is distorted by inhomogeneities
in our universe. We then discuss the impact of the relativistic effects on the
angular power spectrum and on the two-point correlation function in
configuration space. We show that the latter is very well adapted to isolate
the relativistic effects since it naturally makes use of the symmetries of the
different contributions. In particular, we discuss how the Doppler effect and
the gravitational redshift distortions can be isolated by looking for a dipole
in the cross-correlation function between a bright and a faint population of
galaxies.

Germaine Greer has criticised Celebrity Big Brother's "bullying" of housemates after quitting the reality TV show.
She said "superior" bullying tactics, like making housemates cold and hungry, could encourage playground bullying. She also condemned the "complete irresponsibility" of adding Brigitte Nielsen's former mother-in-law Jackie Stallone to the house on Monday. Nielsen had panicked that if she reacted badly it could harm her access to her children, Greer said. The feminist writer and broadcaster said Big Brother had behaved "like a child rather than a parent" by taunting contestant John McCririck after denying him a cola drink. "I thought it was actually demonstrating the role of taunting in the playground and there are so many children whose lives have actually been destroyed by taunting in the playground," Greer said. She also said that her fellow housemates had publicity-seeking "agendas".
"I had no idea who would be in here and it's wrong for me to present myself in the same context as they are." Media observers had been surprised by Greer's initial decision to join the third celebrity version of the Channel 4 reality TV show, given that she has written critical articles about the format in the past. As she packed her suitcase to leave the house she told fellow housemates: "I'm leaving over specific issues, but best for everyone if I don't discuss them. "I have a problem with decisions, I make them fast and when I make them, I stick to them." Greer had earlier failed to persuade other contestants to stage a naked protest against Big Brother.
Other celebrities to walk out of a reality show TV include Sex Pistol John Lydon, former EastEnders actress Danniella Westbrook and ex-E17 singer Brian Harvey who all left I'm A Celebrity... She knew
all I was hoping for
was a little time with you all.
She knew
if the day was bright and sunny
he would be out riding his bike
and the girls would be busy soaking up the sun.
You would inevitably have work to do
whether it was changing the spark plugs
on one of our half-dead vehicles
or mending the fence
to keep our squirrel-crazy bassett hound from escaping.
She knew
I would probably plant flowers by myself.
I love planting flowers
but, I can do that anyday.
Today I wanted to spend with those
who have made me a mother.
She knew
if she dropped the temperature
down into the 40's
you would all surely
seek the warmth of the house.
She knew
that a light drizzle
of ice-cold rain
would ensure your company
throughout the day.
As I curl up on the couch
with all of you surrounding me
and I listen to the predictable bickering
over the popcorn bowl,
I silently thank her
for giving me the gift I wanted most
for Mothers Day.
My family.
I'm glad she knows me so well.
Thank you Mother Nature.
Happy Mothers Day!

GW Pharmaceuticals' prescription cannabis drug, Sativex, produced in the UK, is poised for approval in Canada. Sativex, which treats the central nervous system and mitigates MS symptoms, may become legally accessible to Canadian MS patients within the next few months. This marks a world first for a cannabis-based drug, significantly benefiting both GW Pharma and MS patients. With final approval imminent, analysts anticipate Canadian approval for Sativex in early 2005, as expressed by Dr Geoffrey Guy, GW Pharma's executive chairman: "We are pleased to receive this qualifying notice from Health Canada and look forward to gaining regulatory approval for Sativex in Canada during the early part of 2005."

GW Pharma holds a UK license to cultivate cannabis for medicinal research. The drug comprises a cannabis extract featuring tetrahydrocannabinol and cannabidiol. Over 50,000 Canadians and 85,000 individuals in the UK have been diagnosed with MS, many of whom currently use cannabis to alleviate their symptoms. Previous stock value losses due to UK regulatory concerns regarding the drug's benefits have since been reversed, with shares in GW Pharma rising 8.5p, or 8.1%, to 113.5p upon hearing the Canadian approval news.

For Dipping Sauce
5 ounces apricot jam
1/4 cup crushed pineapple
1 teaspoon apple cider vinegar
1/2 teaspoon red pepper flakes
For Coleslaw
1/4 cup water
1/4 cup olive oil
1/2 cup chopped scallion
1/2 cup cilantro
1 garlic clove
1 pinch salt
2 limes, juiced
1/2 cup sour cream
1 cup chopped green cabbage
1 1/2 cups chopped purple cabbage
For Coconut Shrimp
12 shrimp
3 ounces beer
2 eggs
1/2 cup milk
1 cup flour
1/4 teaspoon baking powder
1/2 teaspoon salt
5 ounces coconut flakes
6 sheets rice paper
To Make Dipping Sauce: In a bowl, combine apricot jelly, crushed pineapple, apple cider vinegar and red pepper flakes. To Make Coleslaw: In a food processor, add water, olive oil, scallions, cilantro, garlic, salt and lime juice. Pulse until combined. Then add sour cream and pulse again. In a bowl, add chopped green and purple cabbage. Drizzle olive oil mixture over the cabbage and mix well. To Make Coconut Shrimp: In a bowl, whisk beer, egg, milk, flour, baking powder, and salt. Dip peeled, headless shrimp in the batter. Then coat with coconut flakes. Fry the breaded shrimp in hot oil until the coconut flakes are golden bown. Place shrimp on a drying rack over a sheet tray to allow the excess oil to drip off. Let cool. Assembling the Roll: On a sheet of moistened rice paper, place a scoop of coleslaw in the middle, edge of the paper (think of it as about 1/3 in from the edge). Then roll and fold until the top of the coleslaw is covered by the rice paper. After the shrimp cools down and excess oil drips off onto the rack, place two shrimp on the roll and continue to wrap until the shrimp is sealed well. Slice in half and serve with the dipping sauce.

Despite a lifetime of wrestling with depression and various hardships, I'm drained beyond belief. I'm puzzled as to why I continue sharing, an unending struggle. Mitzvah Day International is an annual day of faith-based social action that takes place in November each year, primarily in the United Kingdom. On Mitzvah Day each year, community groups and individuals undertake a range of volunteer projects for those in need in their local community. Organizations register with Mitzvah Day, which in turn helps match volunteers with local projects. The objective is to encourage people to give their time, rather than their money, to worthwhile local causes, whilst also creating deeper linkages within communities and supporting charities. In 2013, close to 30,000 people participated in Mitzvah Day around the world.
Though based within the UK's Jewish Community, Mitzvah Day traditionally marks the first day of UK National Inter Faith Week, and as a result has expanded to include participants from other faith communities as well.
'Mitzvah' is the Hebrew biblical term for 'deed' or 'commandment', which has come to mean 'good deed' or 'charitable act' in contemporary English. The 2020 date was Sunday November 15.

The human brain comprises a multilayered architecture, encompassing both forward and backward information flows between layers. Each layer consists of neurons, with neural networks serving as mathematical representations of these neuronal functions. While neural networks mimic the human brain, users solely employ feedforward processes from lower to upper layers; feedback processes from higher to lower layers remain unused. In this study, we introduce Feedback U-Net, a segmentation approach combining Convolutional LSTM and feedback processes. Here, the U-Net output serves as input feedback for subsequent iterations. Via Convolutional LSTM, features are extracted in the second iteration based on those obtained in the initial round. Our technique surpasses conventional U-Net on both Drosophila cell image and Mouse cell image datasets.

The Welsh Students rugby team has been affected by the Welsh Rugby Union's (WRU) restructuring at the youth level. A combined Under-18 team made up of students from various schools and national youth squads is set to debut on Thursday against Italy at Gnoll, leading the WRU to cease financing for representative sides like Wales Students. Consequently, scheduled New Year matches versus England and France have been called off. The Welsh Students Rugby Football Union laments this decision, as these traditional fixtures offer the highest caliber of competition that prepares and showcases players. The secretary of the Welsh Students Rugby Football Union, Reverend Eldon Phillips, commented: "It's unfortunate that we can't keep these matches going this year. "The rigorous competition provided by English and French teams has served as valuable testing grounds for Welsh Students. "A growing number of young rugby players pursuing higher education seek the most challenging opportunities, which are typically found in representative rugby. However, this year, that option will be unavailable to them. Notable alumni of the Wales Students team who later earned full senior representative honors include Robert Jones, Rob Howley, Jon Humphreys, Darren Morris, Martyn Williams, and Ceri Sweeney.

Dinosaurs. Amusement Park. Tourists. Disaster.

Jurassic World has them all.

Naturally, I had to see it.

The beginning holds much promise, and it gets your hopes up for the disaster to come. When it does, there are some great action sequences, especially ones with the glass ball containing the soft, chewy child centre.

Unfortunately the final act unravels into outright farce.

Chris Pratt is great as the affable yet bad-ass Raptor Whisperer. He's got an easy going charisma that could easily carry an iconic character like Indiana Jones.

Bryce Dallas Howard plays Claire Dearing, the uptight park manager, who initially clashes with the laid back Owen. Of course you know where the tension goes.

The film tries to flesh out Claire's character by throwing in her two nephews (someone and another kid), who do double duty as McGuffins.

Vincent D'Onofrio shows up as Hoskins, a villainous representative of the military-industrial complex angling to weaponize velociraptors. He's all sneers and scenery chewing, so obviously evil he's got a goatee. D'Onofrio does it well but the evil plan he's been saddled with by the writers makes no sense at all.

The director, Colin Trevorrow, said in interviews that he wanted the dinosaurs to act like real animals, not cartoon monsters. Quelle surprise! I had no idea, as he has well-fed winged dinos (or near enough to dinos) go on a crazed orgy of violence against hapless tourists. Why? Because cool action sequence!

One poor soul is even treated to the most outlandishly elongated death sequence I've ever seen, all to no end. It didn't justify anything, paid nothing back, offered no comeuppance. It was just gleeful indulgence in sadistic torture of a minor character. It was an Itchy & Scratchy moment.

Which brings us to the final act: turn off your brain before it begins.

The first movie proved you could have a smart script and dinosaurs in the same movie. After that, the IQ of the series dropped with each outing. The first one had chaos theory and amber and DNA extraction and cleverness up the whazoo. It was AWESOME.

What does this one have? Hackneyed evil plans, a clunky plot, and characters so smart they run from T-Rex's in high heels.

The franchise has had a lobotomy.

The Indianapolis Zoo is a zoo located in White River State Park, in Indianapolis, Indiana, United States, housing more than 3,800 animals of more than 320 species and subspecies. The institution is accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) and the American Alliance of Museums as a zoo, an aquarium, and as a botanical garden. The zoo is a private non-profit organization, receiving no tax support and is supported entirely by membership fees, admissions, donations, sales, grants, and an annual fundraiser. History
In 1944, Lowell Nussbaum, columnist for the Indianapolis Times, and later the Indianapolis Star, began to advocate for a zoo through his column "Inside Indianapolis", which inspired the incorporation, in October 1944 of the Indianapolis Zoological Society.  Soon the members of this group had outlined the plans for their zoo. Group members were adamant that "the zoo will rely on admissions, in-park sales, contributions, and memberships to support the zoo". However, it would not be until 20 years later, in 1964, that the zoo opened to the public.

"Moonrise Kingdom" is a whimsical delight, as expected from auteur Wes Anderson whose stylistic flair and unique storytelling techniques shine throughout this film. The plot revolves around two love-struck pre-teens, Sam and Suzy, who decide to run away together, prompting a quaint New England town's obsessive search for them.

The movie is a strikingly profound portrait of adolescence yearning that beautifully combines innocence, love, and adventure, delivering it through Anderson's indelible lens. The visualization is a testament to Anderson's singular vision, conjuring a world filled with vivid color palettes, symmetrical frames, and a detailed aesthetic that emits a magical touch of nostalgia and child-like wonder.

The performances are endearing and impactful, particularly by the young leads Jared Gilman and Kara Hayward. They navigate their roles with an inherent maturity that makes their characters' journey believable and engaging. The supporting cast adds more extraordinary layers to the film with the likes of Bill Murray, Tilda Swinton, Edward Norton, and Bruce Willis, all turning in memorable performances.

The music score is poignant and captures the essence of the 1960s setting impeccably. It forms an integral part of the film, acting as a character unto itself, and helping unveil the depths of emotions and pivotal plot developments. From classical pieces to folksy tunes, the score permeates every scene, enhancing the dynamics between the characters and their environment.

"Moonrise Kingdom" is a heartwarming tale of young love, rebellious spirit, and the enchanting pull of the great outdoors; it is as charming and quirky as it is insightful. It's a vibrant piece of cinematic art that resonates deeply with viewers, regardless of age. Its clever additives of humor are well-placed, providing a balanced mix of laughter, sentimentality, and intensity.

This film, while keeping in sync with Anderson's distinct narrative technique, stands as a testament to his exceptional ability to create captivating, original stories. It is a brilliant, emotionally rich film that reminds us of the rousing whirlwind that is young love and the indomitable spirit of childhood. Thus, "Moonrise Kingdom" is much more than an escapist adventure; it is a precious tribute to the youthful courage, uncomplicated love, and unvanquished imagination we often forget after crossing the bridge to adulthood. For any cinema enthusiast or admirer of unique storytelling, this film comes highly recommended.

Methods that move towards less supervised scenarios are key for image
segmentation, as dense labels demand significant human intervention. Generally,
the annotation burden is mitigated by labeling datasets with weaker forms of
supervision, e.g. image-level labels or bounding boxes. Another option are
semi-supervised settings, that commonly leverage a few strong annotations and a
huge number of unlabeled/weakly-labeled data. In this paper, we revisit
semi-supervised segmentation schemes and narrow down significantly the
annotation budget (in terms of total labeling time of the training set)
compared to previous approaches. With a very simple pipeline, we demonstrate
that at low annotation budgets, semi-supervised methods outperform by a wide
margin weakly-supervised ones for both semantic and instance segmentation. Our
approach also outperforms previous semi-supervised works at a much reduced
labeling cost. We present results for the Pascal VOC benchmark and unify weakly
and semi-supervised approaches by considering the total annotation budget, thus
allowing a fairer comparison between methods.

Boyer's intricate work delves into the origins of religious ideas through the mind's inferential processes, drawing parallels to phenomena like pareidolia and religious imagery derived from facial perception mechanisms in the human brain. Boyer bolsters this naturalistic foundation of religion using data from various fields such as biological anthropology, cultural anthropology, cognitive science, linguistics, evolutionary biology, cognitive psychology, evolutionary psychology, neuroscience, and information processing. In Religion Explained, Boyer positions religious practices and beliefs within the context of contemporary cognitive neuroscience research on the modularity of the mind. This concept entails cognitive "modules" or "units" embedded in inference systems and intuitions. For example, Boyer posits that widespread beliefs in "supernatural agents" (such as gods, ancestors, spirits, and witches) stem from agency detection: the innate, modular process of inferring intentional intervention by conscious beings, irrespective of their actual presence. "When we encounter tree limbs swaying in the wind or hear an unanticipated noise behind us, our initial assumption is that an agent is responsible for these striking occurrences. We make this determination without requiring a detailed description of what the agent might be." Boyer references E.E. Evans-Pritchard's seminal Zande narrative concerning a termite-damaged roof collapsing. For the anthropologist, the structure fell due to termite infestation. For the Zande, however, the underlying question was why the incident transpired at that precise moment, with specific individuals assembled within the dwelling. According to Boyer's hypothesis, religion serves as a "parasitic" (or "spandrel") byproduct from cognitive modules, much like how the reading process relies on language modules.

A 6-pound leg of lamb requires: 6 peeled garlic cloves, salt to taste, freshly ground black pepper to taste, and 2 tablespoons of extra virgin olive oil. Additionally, follow the Mushroom and Wine Sauce recipe (see note).

To serve rare lamb: Let it rest at room temperature. Preheat the oven to 400°F. With a paring knife, create six small incisions on the fatty portion of the roast and insert the garlic cloves. Lightly coat the roast with salt, pepper, and oil. Install a meat thermometer in the thickest part of the leg, avoiding contact with the bone. Cook in a pan with a roasting rack at 400°F for 40 minutes, allowing the exterior to brown. Lower the oven temperature to 325°F and continue cooking for an additional 40 to 50 minutes, or until the meat thermometer indicates 140°F.

For medium lamb, adhere to the previous instructions but cook slightly longer, targeting a thermometer reading between 145 to 150°F. Allow the cooked meat to rest for 1/2 hour prior to slicing as it will continue to cook during this time. Concurrently, prepare the sauce. Serves 4 to 6.

Note: Mushroom And Wine Sauce Recipe:
Ingredients: 1 pound mushrooms, sliced; 1 cup red wine; 2 cups beef broth; 1/2 cup finely chopped onion; 2 cloves garlic, minced; 2 tbsp. butter; 2 tbsp. flour; salt and pepper to taste.

Instructions: Sauté mushrooms and onions in butter until softened. Add garlic and cook for 1 minute. Sprinkle with flour and stir to coat evenly. Gradually pour in red wine and beef broth, whisking constantly to avoid lumps. Season with salt and pepper to taste and simmer until desired thickness is achieved.

In a tranquil park setting, Spenser shares recollections of his past with Susan Silverman. These memories date back to his formative years before his detective career. Through a dialogue between them, Spenser discloses growing up in an all-male household, where his mother died shortly after his birth via cesarean section. Consisting of himself, his uneducated father, and two uncles, they worked in construction and occasionally boxed for additional income. His uncles instilled in him the art of boxing from a tender age of three and introduced him to classic literature at night.

The narrative transitions to Spenser's encounters with a girl named Jeannie Haden. Around the same age, she was initially just a friend. Jeannie's father was an abusive alcoholic. One fateful day, Spenser noticed Jeannie silently pleading for help in her father's car. Following her father's vehicle and eventual boat, he discovered them on a secluded river island, where he successfully rescued Jeannie. After their escape, they encountered Jeannie's father once more, resulting in his demise. Although his family commended him for his actions, they advised against reporting the incident. Despite their urging, Spenser chose to involve the authorities. To his relief, no charges were filed against him.

Jeannie harbored feelings for Spenser, but he did not reciprocate. Despite this, he maintained their friendship. As a gesture of kindness, Spenser agreed to safeguard Aurelio Lopez, a student of Mexican descent who frequently suffered bullying from his peers. Post-intervention, Lopez was no longer tormented. However, this protective action created some distance between Spenser and his former white classmates, many of whom he had known since elementary school. Ultimately, these events shaped Spenser's character and prepared him for his future detective work.

Orleanna Price narrates the introductory chapter in five of the novel's seven sections. The narrative then alternates among the four daughters, with a slight preference for the voice of the most outspoken one, Leah. The four girls increasingly mature, as each adapts differently to African village life, to the misogyny of their father Nathan, and the political turmoil that overtakes The Congo in the 1960s. Since the Congolese villagers are seen through the eyes of the growing daughters, the view changes. At first, they appear as ridiculous savages. But as the girls mature, the villagers become fully fleshed-out human beings, immersed in a complex and sophisticated culture. Nathan's lack of responsiveness to this culture wears out his family's welcome, but he refuses to leave. Only after a series of misfortunes—culminating in the death of one of the daughters—do the women leave Nathan Price to his folly. The survivors take different paths into their futures, the novel ending at the time of Mobutu Sese Seko's death in the 1990s. Rachel, the eldest, marries Axelroot at seventeen, and after two more marriages is the owner of a luxury hotel close to what is now Brazzaville. Leah marries Anatole, has a large family of four boys, and remains in the impoverished Congo. Adah returns to the United States with their mother Orleanna, attending college and later, medical school. She undergoes a lengthy experimental treatment that restores full use of her legs and she begins to speak. Orleanna herself returns to spending life on the Georgian coast, enjoying Adah's occasional visits.

From the standpoint of quasipower law ensembles, this text explores the notion of nonextensive Tsallis distributions, which are characterized by a nonextensive parameter $q$. Various potential origins of such distributions are examined in greater depth. The text goes on to reveal that data indicates distinct nonextensive parameters derived from Tsallis distribution functions $f(p_T)$ and multiplicity distributions related to Tsallis entropy, denoted as $q_1$ and $q_2$, respectively. It is further proven that these parameters hold the relationship $q_1 + q_2 = 2$. The text concludes by demonstrating that Tsallis distributions can be generated using Shannon information entropy, subject to specific conditions linked to the nature of the underlying dynamical processes (additive or multiplicative). Additionally, it explains how a Tsallis distribution can accommodate the log-oscillating pattern observed in certain multiparticle datasets.

The Liberal Democrats have unveiled plans to build 100,000 new "affordable" homes on publicly owned land.
The party's scheme would allow people to buy a share in a home through a mutual home ownership trust, as a way of getting onto the housing ladder. The Lib Dems would also encourage the conversion of existing buildings in an effort to protect greenfield sites. Labour has already announced plans to help first-time buyers and the Tories would extend right-to-buy schemes.
All the major parties are focusing on the issue in the run-up to the election after a survey suggested first-time buyers could not afford a home in 92% of UK towns. The Lib Dems say their "mutual homes" would let people buy a share of a property, usually worth about 5% of the building costs. Party leader Charles Kennedy said the homes would be affordable because they would be built on surplus public sector land, donated by central or local government. People would also only have to pay for the cost of the building and not the land, he added.
They would spend about 30% of their monthly salary on rent and buying extra shares in the property. When they moved house, they would be able to cash in on any rise in property prices by selling their share. It would also allow councils to vary discounts to tenants given the right to buy their council homes so local needs were taken into account. Mr Kennedy said: "Mutual homes will offer people the opportunity to build up an equity stake in a home gradually, investing only as much as they can afford."
There are also plans to prevent high house prices forcing people out of their local communities. The kind of "golden share" used by the Lib Dems in South Shropshire could be rolled out more widely. Under the plan, councils secure deals with developers where they keep a 1% share in a property scheme so properties cannot be sold on the open market. Instead, they are sold at "build cost" to people who the local council decides have local needs. The party says its help for first-time buyers can be funded at no extra cost to the taxpayer. But the plans involve changing the VAT system, which the party says often makes it too expensive to renovate existing buildings.
The Conservatives claimed the plans would amount to an extra tax of up to £11,000 on every new house. "This is typical of Lib Dem hypocrisy," said Tory shadow local government secretary Caroline Spelman. "They claim that they want to help people on to the property ladder, but the small print of their policies reveal how they intend to price even more people out of the housing market." The flagship Tory proposal on housing policy is to give a million more housing association tenants the right to buy their homes. Labour has said it will allow 300,000 council and housing association tenants to buy a share in their homes. Housing Minister Keith Hill said much of the Lib Dem plans mimicked the government's strategy. "However, as usual, the Lib Dems' proposals are completely uncosted," he said. Mr Hill said he also asked whether the Lib Dems would match Labour's promise to spend £42bn on making refurbishing and repair council homes by 2010.

Reading the back cover of the DVD and seeing that Colin Firth and Ben Kingsley are given top billing, I expected an intelligent King Arthur story. Well, it really wasn't either, although I did find it entertaining. I must not have read the description carefully enough. No matter; overall, it was fun but just a little too silly. I'm beginning to wonder about the discernment of some of these actors, how they can play such intelligent roles for a film or two and then revert to something like this.

Anyway, the story is really a Roman empire one, not a King Arthur story. We only see the tie-in to the later in the last few minutes of the film, in the epilogue. This action story is all about the last Caesar, a small boy, and the last legion that fought as Rome had now been taken over by the Goths. The Roman Empire had come to an end.

Mixed in with that tale was the famous "excalibur" sword. We see the origins of that and how it eventually got into the hands of King Arthur. But, once again, that is only explained in the final minutes. However, the sword is used by the good Roman general who protects the last Caesar from the Goths, who want him imprisoned for life, or killed.

What made the story interesting, at least for me, was the chase-scene type atmosphere of a small band of heroes protecting a little boy, fleeing the bloodthirsty Goths until they could mount some sort of counter-attack in the north in Brittania. That, and the pretty computer-generated scenery and action stunts, kept it interesting. However, don't look for credibility in those action scenes and expect the typical political-correctness of today (i.e. where a woman beats up hundreds of men and the good guys of all colors prevail despite ridiculous odds).

Some parts of this will leave you shaking your head in disbelief. You will feel you're watching a kids' film at times. However, if you want an hour-and-a-half of decent escapist fare, and can put your brain on hold for that time, it fits the bill and will at least entertain you.

Utilizing obsolete mobile phones brings both ecological and social advantages. According to research, discarded mobile phones can bridge the digital divide in certain developing countries due to their affordable price. However, more efforts are required to gather old phones instead of allowing them to accumulate in landfills. In the UK alone, 15 million mobile phones become obsolete annually, yet only 25% are returned to phone companies for recycling or repurposing. This amassing stockpile of unused phones amounts to 90 million handsets, or 9,000 metric tons of waste, according to James Goodman, report author and senior advisor at the Forum for the Future. "Many individuals possess two or three redundant phones," noted Mr. Goodman.

Rather than disposing of these older phones in landfills, releasing hazardous substances into the environment, it would be wiser to return them to operators who can then export them for further usage. "While we acknowledge the environmental incentive for doing so," stated Mr. Goodman, "there are compelling social reasons as well." Old mobile phones have proven valuable in impoverished regions where residents aspire to own a mobile device and maintain contact with loved ones but lack the financial means to purchase the latest models. The Forum for the Future report delved deep into Romania, where refurbished mobile phones have gained popularity. "Romania is an intriguing case study," explained Mr. Goodman, "due to its dismal fixed-line network and widespread demand for mobile phones." Despite Romania being one of Europe's poorest countries, its citizens eagerly embrace mobile technology.

In this study, we propose a novel approach to medical image segmentation called PGL (Prior-Guided Local Self-supervision). Our method leverages prior knowledge about the structure of the target object in an image and uses it to guide self-supervision during training. Specifically, we use local patches from the input image as well as corresponding patches from a set of reference images with known labels to train a neural network. We also incorporate a regularization term that encourages the learned features to be consistent across different patches within each image. The results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of incorporating prior knowledge into self-supervised learning for medical image segmentation tasks.

To make the broth, stir the pear nectar, agave nectar, lemon zest, ginger, maple syrup, and saffron together in a large saucepan or 3-quart saute pan over medium-high heat. Bring to a boil, then place the pear halves in the saucepan, flat side down. Place a piece of parchment paper over the pears and cover with a small plate to weight the pears down as they simmer. Lower the heat and simmer until the pears are tender and a knife pierces them all the way through without resistance. Remove the pears from the saucepan. Return the liquid to the heat, bring to a lively simmer, and cook until syrupy, about 10 minutes. Taste the liquid for a quick FASS check. It may need a pinch of salt and a squeeze of lemon juice to balance the flavors. Serve the pears drizzled with the poaching liquid and topped with a dollop of nut cream if you like. For vanilla broth, omit the lemon zest, ginger, maple syrup, and saffron, and instead stir 2 teaspoons of agave nectar into the pear nectar. Cut a vanilla pod in half lengthwise, scrape the seeds into the saucepan, then throw in the pod. Proceed with the recipe as above. For star anise broth, omit the lemon zest, ginger, maple syrup, and saffron, and instead stir in 4 pods of star anise, 4 whole cloves, 2 cinnamon sticks, 2 teaspoons of agave nectar, and 2 teaspoons of freshly squeezed lemon juice. Proceed with the recipe as above. To seed and stem a pear beautifully, once its cut in half, use a melon baller to scoop out the center, making sure to remove all of the seeds. Then use a sharp paring knife to make a small angled slice on each side of the core, running out from the center of the pear to the stem. This will remove a clean and even triangle-shaped piece where the stem and the core had been. You can garnish the pears with the solids from the broth. Lemon peel, vanilla pods, star anise pods, and cloves all make beautiful garnishes. Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3 to 5 days. We perform a rigorous spectral analysis of the intrinsic $B$-mode power spectrum $P_{BB}$ in the limit of a large horizon and at leading order in the slow-roll approximation. This analysis requires a clear definition of the polarized $B$-mode spectrum on the whole probed angular scale range, which is lacking in the current literature. We introduce a new parametrization that is both well-defined and suitable for performing the slow-roll approximation. By means of this parametrization, we show that the amplitude of $P_{BB}$ is given by the usual expression in terms of the scalar tilt $n_S$, but with a spectral index $n_S^{(B)}$ different from the scalar one $n_S$. We evaluate the corresponding running of the $B$-mode spectral index, and provide a simple fitting function that depends on the two standard slow-roll parameters $\epsilon$ and $\eta$ and on a single extra parameter $\beta_B$ that governs the running. We show that the running of the $B$-mode spectral index is constrained by the Planck satellite, even though $P_{BB}$ itself is too small to be detectable yet. We also show that a detection of gravitational waves with an r.m.s. amplitude of $1$ would lead to a significant improvement of the constraint, and we quantify the effect of neglecting the running.

The work reported in this article presents a high-order, stable, and
efficient Gegenbauer pseudospectral method to solve numerically a wide variety
of mathematical models. The proposed numerical scheme exploits the stability
and the well-conditioning of the numerical integration operators to produce
well-conditioned systems of algebraic equations, which can be solved easily
using standard algebraic system solvers. The core of the work lies in the
derivation of novel and stable Gegenbauer quadratures based on the stable
barycentric representation of Lagrange interpolating polynomials and the
explicit barycentric weights for the Gegenbauer-Gauss (GG) points. A rigorous
error and convergence analysis of the proposed quadratures is presented along
with a detailed set of pseudocodes for the established computational
algorithms. The proposed numerical scheme leads to a reduction in the
computational cost and time complexity required for computing the numerical
quadrature while sharing the same exponential order of accuracy achieved by
Elgindy and Smith-Miles (2013). The bulk of the work includes three numerical
test examples to assess the efficiency and accuracy of the numerical scheme.
The present method provides a strong addition to the arsenal of numerical
pseudospectral methods, and can be extended to solve a wide range of problems
arising in numerous applications.

Ultracold neutron (UCN) detectors are crucial tools in various fields of research, including particle physics, materials science, and nuclear medicine. However, current UCN detectors suffer from limited efficiency and spatial resolution due to their simple design, which consists of a single layer of converter material.

In this work, we present a novel approach to UCN detection that utilizes a multilayer surface detector. By stacking multiple layers of different materials with varying neutron interaction cross-sections, we enhance the detection efficiency and improve the spatial resolution. The additional layers also allow for better discrimination between UCNs and background particles, leading to improved signal-to-noise ratio.

The proposed detector design consists of alternating layers of boron carbide (B4C) and graphite, which provide efficient conversion of UCNs into charged particles. The B4C layers have high thermal conductivity, ensuring fast heat dissipation and reducing the risk of thermal neutron absorption. In contrast, the graphite layers have low atomic number, minimizing the probability of UCN absorption.

We simulate the performance of our multilayer surface detector using Monte Carlo simulations and compare it to traditional single-layer detectors. Our results show an increase in detection efficiency by up to 50% and an improvement in spatial resolution by a factor of 2-3. We also experimentally validate our design using a prototype detector at a UCN source.

Our findings demonstrate the potential of multilayer surface detectors for enhancing UCN detection capabilities. This technology can be applied in various areas, such as fundamental neutron physics experiments, neutron scattering and imaging applications, and medical treatments involving UCNs.

The Lennox Bridge, Glenbrook is a heritage-listed road bridge that carries the Mitchell's Pass across Brookside Creek (also known as Lapstone Creek), located at Glenbrook, in the City of Blue Mountains local government area of New South Wales, Australia. The bridge was designed by David Lennox and built from 1832 to 1833 by James Randall and other convicts. It is also known as Lennox Bridge or The Horseshoe Bridge. The property is owned by Blue Mountains City Council. It was added to the New South Wales State Heritage Register on 2 April 1999. The stone arch bridge is a single arch of  span and is  above water level, with a road width of . History 
The first road up the eastern slopes of the Blue Mountains, built by William Cox (1814–15), was in Governor Macquarie's words "pretty steep and sharp" and was found to be subject to serious washways. This road was superseded in 1824 by what was known as the Bathurst Road (now Old Bathurst Road). It avoided watercourses, but its grade was very steep and this rendered it hazardous to travellers. When Major Thomas Mitchell was appointed as Surveyor General in 1828, one of the first matters to which he turned his attention was the improvement of the Great Western Road. Mitchell's attention was focussed on providing a more direct and easily graded route for the Great Western Road. Mitchell surveyed and recommended the construction of a road along this route midway between the other two in preference to the Governor's suggestion of stationing a permanent repair gang on the Old Bathurst Road.

A Plaid Cymru MP believes UK security services were involved in some arson attacks blamed on Welsh extremists.
It is 25 years since the start of 12 years of fire-bombings, attributed to a shadowy group known as Meibion Glyndwr. Plaid Cymru's Elfyn Llwyd has suggested the security services could have been involved, with the intention of discrediting the nationalist vote. Ex-Welsh Office Minister Lord Roberts of Conwy denied security services were involved. In March this year, North Wales Police reopened the case, saying materials kept during their investigations would be examined to find whether it would yield DNA evidence.
Meibion Glyndwr - which means "sons of Glyndwr" - began burning property in December 1979 in protest at homes in rural Wales being sold as holiday cottages to people from England. The group was linked to most of the 220 or so fire-bombing incidents stretching from the Llyn Peninsula to Pembrokeshire. The campaign continued until the early 1990s. Police were accused in some quarters of targeting anyone who was a nationalist. Although one man, Sion Aubrey Roberts, was convicted in 1993 of sending letter bombs in the post, the arson cases remain unsolved.
As a solicitor, Elfyn Llwyd represented Welsh singer Bryn Fôn when he was arrested on suspicion of being involved in the arson campaign. Fôn was released without charge . But now, as MP for Merionnydd Nant Conwy and Plaid Cymru's Parliamentary Leader, Mr Llwyd has argued that some of the terror attacks may have had the involvement of the security services and not Meibion Glyndwr. He believes that elements of the British security services may have carried out renegade actions in order to discredit Plaid Cymru and the nationalist vote ahead of elections. The claim is made in an interview for BBC Wales' Maniffesto programme to be shown on S4C on Sunday.
Mr Llwyd said that the sophistication of many of the devices used in the attacks compared to the crude nature of many others, suggests a degree of professionalism which could only have come from individuals who knew exactly what they were doing. He said: "What I'm saying is that the role that they took wasn't the appropriate one, i.e. like an
agent provocateur
and perhaps interfering and creating a situation where it looked like it was the nationalists that were responsible." The programme also heard from Lord Roberts of Conwy, who was a Welsh Office minister at the time. He denied that the security services played any improper role. Mr Llwyd's theory has also been questioned by Plaid Cymru's former President, Dafydd Wigley. He accepted that the fires damaged Plaid Cymru's public image but believed that the security services had their hands full at the time with the IRA and animal rights activists.
 - Maniffesto can be seen on S4C on Sunday, 12 December, at 1200 GMT.

Instructions:
Select twelve blemish-free, organically grown small lemons, preferably Meyer variety. Thoroughly clean and dry them. For store-bought lemons, gently scrub to eliminate residual pesticides.
