Liah Greenfeld (born 1952) is an American sociologist and historian. She is a Professor of Sociology and an Affiliate of the Center for International Affairs at Harvard University. Greenfeld is the author of Nationalism: Five Roads to Modernity (1992), The Spirit of Capitalism (2001), mind, modernity, madness: the impact of culture on human experience (2013), among other books.

Greenfeld was born in New York City and raised on Long Island. She attended Brandeis University, where she received a B.A. in sociology in 1974. She then went on to earn a Ph.D. in sociology from the University of California, Berkeley in 1980.

Greenfeld's research interests include nationalism, sociological theory, the history of capitalism, and the sociology of culture. She is the author of Nationalism: Five Roads to Modernity (1992), The Spirit of Capitalism (2001), and mind, modernity, madness: the impact of culture on human experience (2013).

Abstract:
Sematic segmentation is a computer vision task that has been widely used in various applications such as object detection, image captioning, and video analysis. However, the performance of semantic segmentation models heavily depends on the amount and quality of training data and annotations. In this paper, we investigate the problem of limited data and annotations in semantic segmentation and propose several methods to overcome this limitation. First, we explore the use of transfer learning from pre-trained models and show that it can improve the performance of semantic segmentation on limited data. Second, we propose a method to generate synthetic data and annotations using generative adversarial networks (GANs) and demonstrate that it can effectively augment the training data. Finally, we present a new loss function that combines both global and local information to improve the performance of semantic segmentation on data with limited annotations. The experimental results show that our methods can significantly improve the performance of semantic segmentation on limited data and annotations.

The story begins in Prague with news of the assassination in Sarajevo that precipitates World War I. Švejk displays such enthusiasm about faithfully serving the Austrian Emperor in battle that no one can decide whether he is merely an imbecile or is craftily undermining the war effort. However, he is arrested by a member of the secret police, Bretschneider, after making some politically sensitive remarks, and is sent to prison. After being certified insane he is transferred to a madhouse, before being ejected. Švejk gets his charwoman to wheel him (he claims to be suffering from rheumatism) to the recruitment offices in Prague, where his apparent zeal causes a minor sensation. Unfortunately, he is transferred to a hospital for malingerers because of his rheumatism. He finally joins the army as batman to army chaplain Otto Katz; Katz loses him at cards to Lieutenant Lukáš, whose batman he then becomes. Lukáš is posted with his march battalion to barracks in České Budějovice, in Southern Bohemia, preparatory to being sent to the front. After missing the train to Budějovice, Švejk embarks on a long anabasis on foot around Southern Bohemia in a vain attempt to find Budějovice, before being arrested as a possible spy and deserter (a charge he strenuously denies) and escorted to his regiment. He is then promoted to company orderly. The unit embarks on a long train journey towards Galicia and the Eastern Front. Stopping in a town on the border between Austria and Hungary, in which relations between the two nationalities are somewhat sensitive, Švejk is again arrested, this time for causing an affray involving a respectable Hungarian citizen and engaging in a street fight. After a further long journey and close to the front line, Švejk is taken prisoner by his own side as a suspected Russian deserter, after arriving at a lake and trying on an abandoned Russian uniform. Narrowly avoiding execution, he manages to rejoin his unit. The unfinished novel breaks off abruptly before Švejk has a chance to be involved in any combat or enter the trenches, though it appears Hašek may have conceived that the characters would have continued the war in a POW camp, much as he had done. The book also includes a very large number of anecdotes told by Švejk (usually either to deflect the attentions of an authority figure, or to insult them in a concealed manner) which are not directly related to the plot.

In a parallel universe, England and Imperial Russia have fought the Crimean War for more than a century; England itself is a police state run by the Goliath Corporation (a powerful weapon-producing company with questionable morals); and Wales is a separate, socialist nation. The book's fictional version of Jane Eyre ends with Jane accompanying her cousin, St. John Rivers, to India in order to help him with his missionary work. Literary questions (especially the question of Shakespearean authorship) are debated so hotly that they sometimes inspire gang wars and murder. Single, thirty-six, Crimean War veteran and literary detective Thursday Next lives in London with her pet dodo, Pickwick. As the story begins, Thursday is temporarily promoted to investigate the theft of the original manuscript of Charles Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit because she is one of the few people able to identify the thief, Acheron Hades. She comes close to capturing him during a stakeout, but is badly injured, saved by a copy of Jane Eyre that stops Hades' bullet. A mysterious stranger aids her until the paramedics arrive, leaving behind only a monogrammed handkerchief and jacket. Next recognizes these items as those of Rochester, a character from Jane Eyre, because she entered the novel as a child and briefly became acquainted with Rochester himself while she was there. While recovering in hospital, Thursday is instructed by her future self to take the LiteraTec job in her home town of Swindon. There, she discovers that her Uncle Mycroft has created the Prose Portal, which allows people to enter works of fiction. Next also renews an acquaintance with her former fiancé Landen Parke-Laine (a reference to the British version of the board game Monopoly). Hades kidnaps Mycroft, Polly, and the Prose Portal in order to blackmail the literary world; any changes made to the plot of a novel's original manuscript will change all other copies. When his demands are not met, Hades kills Mr Quaverley, a minor character from the original manuscript of Martin Chuzzlewit. Next and a Goliath Corporation operative named Jack Schitt trace Hades to Wales and rescue Mycroft and the Prose Portal, but find that Polly is stuck in one of Wordsworth's poems and Hades has gone into the original text of Jane Eyre. Next pursues Hades, and after much trouble, succeeds in killing him. In the process, Thornfield Hall is burned, Rochester's mad wife Bertha falls to her death, and Rochester himself is grievously injured (in other words, she alters the ending of the book to match the actual ending to Jane Eyre). Returning to her own world, Next uses the Prose Portal to release her Aunt Polly and imprison Jack Schitt in the text of Edgar Allan Poe's "The Raven". She shows up at the church where Parke-Laine is about to be married to another woman, but a lawyer interrupts the wedding and Next and Parke-Laine are reconciled and marry instead. Next's father, a renegade agent from SpecOps-12, the ChronoGuard, turns up to dispense some fatherly advice to his daughter. The novel ends with Next facing an uncertain future at work: public reaction to the new ending for Jane Eyre is positive, but there are other repercussions.

Video game giant Electronic Arts (EA) says it wants to become the biggest entertainment firm in the world.
The US firm says it wants to compete with companies such as Disney and will only achieve this by making games appeal to mainstream audiences. EA publishes blockbuster titles such as Fifa and John Madden, as well as video game versions of movies such as Harry Potter and the James Bond films. Its revenues were $3bn (£1.65bn) in 2004, which EA hoped to double by 2009. EA is the biggest games publisher in the world and in 2004 had 27 titles which sold in excess of one million copies each. Nine of the 20 biggest-selling games in the UK last year were published by EA.
Gerhard Florin, EA's managing director for European publishing, said: "Doubling our industry in five years is not rocket science." He said it would take many years before EA could challenge Disney - which in 2004 reported revenues of $30bn (£16bn) - but it remained a goal for the company. "We will be able to bring more people into gaming because games will be more emotional." Mr Florin predicted that the next round of games console would give developers enough power to create real emotion.
"It's the subtleties, the eyes, the mouth - 5,000 polygons doesn't really sell the emotion.
"With PS3 and Xbox 2, we can go on the main character with 30,000 to 50,000 polygons," he said. "With that increased firepower, the Finding Nemo video game looks just like the movie, but it will be interactive." Mr Florin said that more than 50% of all EA's games were sold to adults and played by adults, but the perception remained that the video game industry was for children. "Our goal is to bring games to the masses which bring out emotions." EA said the video game industry was now bigger than the music industry. "Nobody queues for music anymore."
"You can't ignore an industry when people queue to buy a game at midnight because they are so desperate to play it," he said, referring to demand for titles for such as Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas and Halo 2.
Jan Bolz, EA's vice president of sales and marketing in Europe, said the firm was working to give video games a more central role in popular culture. He said the company was in advanced stages of discussions over a reality TV show in which viewers could control the actions of the characters as in its popular game The Sims. "One idea could be that you're controlling a family, telling them when to go to the kitchen and when to go to the bedroom, and with this mechanism you have gamers all over the world 'playing the show'," said Mr Bolz.
He also said EA was planning an international awards show "similar to the Oscars and the Grammys" which would combine video games, music and movies. Mr Bolz said video games firm had to work more closely with celebrities. "People will want to play video games if their heroes like Robbie Williams or Christina Aguilera are in them." Mr Florin said the challenge was to keep people playing in their 30s, 40s and 50s. "There's an indication that a 30 year old comes home from work and still wants to play games. "If that's true, that's a big challenge for TV broadcasters - because watching TV is the biggest pastime at present."

The organization of matter is typically denoted by order parameters signifying the kind and extent of arrangement within a given system. Crystals represent one such instance, characterized by a regular lattice of atoms which disintegrates upon melting. Inferentially, in ferromagnets, the magnetic moments of constituent elements synchronize only beneath the Curie temperature, TC. This distinction illuminates two types of phase transitions: the dissolution of a crystal's crystalline structure denotes a first-order transition, whereas the emergence of magnetism in ferromagnets constitutes a second-order transition. Itinerant magnetic phases, however, are uncommon in model itinerant systems due to the mobility of their particles. In this investigation, we delve into the itinerant magnetic phases existing in a spin-1 spin-orbit linked atomic Bose gas. In this setting, itinerant ferromagnetic order arises due to spin-orbit coupling, disappearing when absent. Initially, we identified a continuous second-order phase transition that eventually morphs into a first-order transition at a critical point, exhibiting a narrow observed width (approximately h x 4 Hz). Subsequently, we examined the prolonged metastable states linked to the first-order transition. Our experimental findings align with theoretical predictions.

The London Stock Exchange (LSE) is planning to announce a preferred takeover by the end of the month, newspaper reports claim.
The Sunday Telegraph said the LSE's plan was further evidence it wants to retain tight control over its destiny. Both Deutsche Boerse and rival Euronext held talks with the London market last week over a possible offer. A £1.3bn offer from Deutsche Boerse has already been rejected, while Euronext has said it will make an all cash bid. Speculation suggests that Paris-based Euronext has the facilities in place to make a bid of £1.4bn, while its German rival may up its bid to the £1.5bn mark. Neither has yet tabled a formal bid, but the LSE is expected to hold further talks with the two parties later this week. However, the Sunday Telegraph report added that there are signs that Deutsche Boerse chief executive Werner Seifert is becoming increasingly impatient with the LSE's managed bid process.
Despite insisting he wants to agree a recommended deal with the LSE's board, the newspaper suggested he may pull out of the process and put an offer directly to shareholders instead. The newspaper also claimed Mr Seifert was becoming "increasingly frustrated" with the pace of negotiations since Deutsche Boerse's £1.3bn offer was rejected in mid-December, in particular the LSE's decision to suspend talks over the Christmas period. Meanwhile, the German exchange's offer has come under fire recently. Unions for Deutsche Boerse staff in Frankfurt have reportedly expressed fears that up to 300 jobs would be moved to London if the takeover is successful. Others claim it will weaken the city's status as Europe's financial centre, while German politicians are also said to be angry over the market operator's promise to move its headquarters to London if a bid is successful. A further stumbling block is Deutsche Boerse's control over its Clearstream unit, the clearing house that processes securities transactions. LSE shareholders fear it would create a monopoly situation, weakening the position of shareholders when negotiating lower transaction fees for share dealings. LSE and Euronext do not have control over their clearing and settlement operations, a situation which critics say is more transparent and competitive.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C). Wrap one sweet potato in parchment paper and aluminum foil. Prick it multiple times with a fork before baking it for about an hour. Allow it to cool once done. Decrease the oven temperature to 350°F (180°C). In the meantime, wrap the remaining sweet potatoes in foil and bake them alongside the first one for around 45 minutes. Once tender, remove their skins. Thinly slice three sweet potatoes using a mandoline or sharp knife, yielding 30 slices. Cut each slice into rectangles measuring 2 inches by 4 inches. Fill a large pot with water and bring it to a boil. Cook half of the sweet potato slices until softened, which should take about 2 minutes. Remove them with a slotted spoon and set them aside to cool slightly. Repeat this process with the remaining slices. Mash the cooked sweet potato from the previously baked one in a food processor until completely smooth. Combine this with the cottage cheese in the food processor and blend until they form a uniform mixture. Transfer the potato-cheese mixture to a large bowl. Stir in the diced apples, chopped chives, grated Parmesan, salt, and pepper. Grease a 9x13 inch baking dish with oil. Spoon about 1 heaping tablespoon of the filling onto the center of a sweet potato slice and roll it up tightly. Arrange the rolls, seam side down, in the prepared baking dish. From a novel viewpoint, we explore boosting algorithms. Through analyzing their Lagrange dual problems, we demonstrate that AdaBoost, LogitBoost, and soft-margin LPBoost with generalized hinge loss are equivalent to entropy maximization issues. Our investigation reveals that boosting algorithms' effectiveness stems from optimally distributing margins while managing margin fluctuation through this method. Furthermore, we establish that approximately, AdaBoost maximizes the mean margin rather than the minimal margin. The duality formulation provides a basis for developing column generation optimization techniques, which yield classification outcomes nearly identical to those of traditional stage-wise additive boosting algorithms yet boast significantly quicker convergence speeds. Consequently, fewer weak classifiers are required when constructing an ensemble using our suggested optimization strategy.

Citrus segmentation is a key step of automatic citrus picking. While most
current image segmentation approaches achieve good segmentation results by
pixel-wise segmentation, these supervised learning-based methods require a
large amount of annotated data, and do not consider the continuous temporal
changes of citrus position in real-world applications. In this paper, we first
train a simple CNN with a small number of labelled citrus images in a
supervised manner, which can roughly predict the citrus location from each
frame. Then, we extend a state-of-the-art unsupervised learning approach to
pre-learn the citrus's potential movements between frames from unlabelled
citrus's videos. To take advantages of both networks, we employ the multimodal
transformer to combine supervised learned static information and unsupervised
learned movement information. The experimental results show that combing both
network allows the prediction accuracy reached at 88.3$\%$ IOU and 93.6$\%$
precision, outperforming the original supervised baseline 1.2$\%$ and 2.4$\%$.
Compared with most of the existing citrus segmentation methods, our method uses
a small amount of supervised data and a large number of unsupervised data,
while learning the pixel level location information and the temporal
information of citrus changes to enhance the segmentation effect.

The story of Earthsearch 2 continues the adventures of the crew of the starship Challenger (Telson, Sharna, Darv and Astra) begun in the previous serial, Earthsearch, which told the story of theirquest for their lost ancestral homeplanet of Earth (which had moved to orbit a new and unknown star when its citizens realised their original sun was going to go nova). At the end of the serial, the four crewmembers had chosen to settle on the sufficiently Earth-like planet Paradise and escape the ruthless, manipulative control of the Challengers megalomaniacal control computers, Angel One and Angel Two. While the Angels departed Paradise orbit to continue the Earthsearch mission (and to achieve their aim of dominating an entire civilisation), the humans began their new life on their new homeworld. Earthsearch 2 begins four years later, when Telson, Sharna, Darv and Astra have settled into their life on Paradise (assisted by two androids, the agricultural machine George and the argumentative general-purpose service unit Tidy). Both couples now have young children - Darv and Astra have the twins Elka and Savin, and Telson and Sharna have their son Bran. Despite the colonists' embrace of Paradise as home, the lifestyle is proving to be difficult and full of hardships. Sharna's loss of what would have been her second child raises questions about the sustainability of the small colony as well as bringing up differences of opinion on how (and whether) to use the remaining technology and resources (including their surviving planetary shuttle). When Savin is unexpectedly killed by a 'monster' that appears from the sea, the colonists are placed under further strain. Noticing the appearance of an unidentified artefact in planetary orbit, Telson and Darv fly up towards it in the shuttle, to discover that it is an eight-mile long spaceship called Voyager 30 and apparently part of an Earth-originated survey mission. Appearances are deceptive. The spaceship is in fact the returning Challenger: repaired, shortened, refitted and still operated by the Angels (as well by a team of control room androids overseen by Android Surgeon-General Kraken). The Angels are now being attacked by mysterious transmissions apparently aimed at damaging or destroying organic computers such as themselves and the Challengers higher intelligence androids. As humans are totally unaffected by the attacks, the Angels require human assistance in order to seek out and destroy the transmissions at source, and have therefore returned to Paradise to recruit the only humans they can obtain. However, the Angels do not reveal this information, and instead feign an interest in the welfare of the colony in an attempt to gain the trust of the humans. At the same time they have secretly sent an android to kidnap the children (the same "sea monster" which accidentally killed Savin in a bungled abduction attempt). When rejected by the suspicious humans, the Angels resort to sabotage on a planetary scale, using terraforming equipment from the Challenger to melt Paradise's polar ice caps and thus raise the sea level in an attempt to get their former crew to rejoin them on the ship. The resulting flooding begins to submerge all of the land, forcing the settlers to abandon their colony and use their shuttle as a floating ark, even down to loading breeding pairs of animals into the shuttle cargo bay. The crew survive and hold out against the Angels' plans until a series of accidents loses them their drinking water, forcing a surrender. They make the best of things by demanding a concession in the shape of a reversal of the flood (so that the animals can be released and survive), following which they fly their shuttle up to the Challenger. On board the Challenger, the colonists make attempts to regain control over both the Angels and the ships control room, but are thwarted when the Angels kidnap the children from the shuttle. The adults are gassed by a surgical android and fall unconscious. When they come round, they discover that the ship has long left the Paradise system and that they have been in suspended animation for sixteen years. However, the children have been awake the whole time, and have aged normally, now being between eighteen and nineteen years old and firmly under the influence of the Angels. Elka appears friendly and enthusiastic, but Bran is now both hostile and the commander of the Challenger. He demonstrates harsh suspicion and aggression towards his parents and the other two adults, even threatening to kill them should they challenge his authority. En route to the source system of the attacks, the Challenger encounters a free-floating fifty-mile wide parabolic dish which the Angels decide to use as raw material for shielding. Telson, Sharna, Darv and Astra are sent to investigate the dish. They discover that it is an abandoned artificial sun called Solaria D, used by the Earth during its transit to its new sun, and presided over by an Angel-like control computer called Solaria. Despite her apparent benevolence, Solaria is revealed to have been abandoned by Earth once she developed murderous megalomaniacal tendencies. Darv succeeds in destroying her. During their stay on Solaria D, the crew discover the name (though not the location) of Earth's new home star, Novita Six. Returning to the Challenger, the crew notice that Solaria D is now moving in an anomalous way. They discover that the artificial sun is now in the grip of the gravity well of a black hole, and that the Challenger is following it. Attempts to escape from the black hole are hampered by the fact that the human crew have no access to the Challengers control room, where Android Surgeon-General Kraken has had his reasoning capacity damaged by the continuing attacks and is no longer responding to or obeying instructions. With the Angels drastically weakened by the attacks and unable to assist, the humans attempt to storm the control room, which is defended by android warriors. The assault fails when the crew run out of time and the Challenger is pulled into the black hole. The crew regain consciousness to find themselves on a gigantic plain surrounded by many different kinds of abandoned starships, including the Challenger. They discover that they have in fact landed unharmed on an enormous artificial construct - a "gravity platform" which merely resembles a black hole and forms part of Earth's long-range defences, acting as a trap for potentially hostile vessels. The chief engineer of Spaceguard Six, Theros, refuses to release either the Challenger or its crew as he deems the Angels too much of a threat. Not only have they integrated themselves into the entire structure of the ship (making their removal from it effectively impossible), Theros suspects that they may have interposed themselves into the brains of the Challengers crew. When Darv locates the Spaceguard's gravitational control room and reverses the field, he frees the Challenger but at the cost of destroying Spaceguard Six. The ship continues its journey, but immediately runs into further problems when debris from the Spaceguard seriously damages the ship's life support systems and farm galleries, threatening the lives of all humans and organic computers on the ship. With the inexperienced and insecure Bran unable to cope (and undermined by Elka, who secretly dominates him and dictates his actions at the prompting of the Angels), Telson regains command of the Challenger and succeeds in organising the crew to deal with the problems. A second assault on the control room is more successful, but attracts the wrath of the near-invincible Android Surgeon-General Kraken, who kidnaps Darv and Astra to replace his destroyed control room androids. Now suffering catastrophic delusions about seizing the power of stars, Kraken is placing the ship at drastic risk. With the assistance of their android Tidy, the crew manage to destroy Kraken and regain control of the ship. Telson discovers that Kraken has coincidentally selected Novita Six as the ship's next target star. Arriving in the Novita Six system, the Challenger finally reaches its original home, Earth. However, the planet does not look like the Earth that the crew have seen in recordings. It is almost totally dead, with very little water and no rain. The only sign of life is a huge ten-mile-high tower on the equator, with a tiny village nearby. The crew fly down to the village, and meet Peeron, the leader. They discover that the Earth's civilisation has collapsed a long time ago, and the human race is reduced to eking out a meagre living from a tiny spring that grows weaker every year. It appears that the humans will be extinct in a short period of time. The Challenger crew use the terraforming systems on the Challenger to bring rain to Earth and create a stable weather pattern which will allow the people to flourish. The crew examine the tower, finding that there is a door set into one side which cannot be opened. Peeron says that many of his predecessors have made attempts over the centuries - for example, by hitting the door with battering rams - but it will not budge. It is said that it is held shut by a "lock of knowledge". Darv eventually works out how to open the ingeniously simple lock, which requires a low grade of technology which would only be available to people who have already worked out basic principles of science and engineering. The door is a very close/accurate fit in the aperture, and contains mild heating elements that cause it to expand and lock in place. These heaters do not heat it to the point that it is warm to the touch. Simply attaching a refrigeration system to the door and cooling it a few degrees causes the door to shrink and move freely. When the crew open the door, they enter the tower, leaving Peeron and his people outside. They discover that the tower contains a colossal library, presided over by the artificial intelligence "Earthvoice" which serves as both the voice of the library and as a "guardian". Earthvoice explains to the crew that the tower was constructed by the people of Earth as a repository of all human knowledge when their last great civilisation was collapsing. The lock was designed so that the people could not enter until they had already worked out how to make some technology for themselves. Unfortunately, Earthvoice's abilities do not included weather control, so although he has successfully defended Earth's legacy of knowledge he has been helpless to deal with the deterioration of the planet's environmental conditions. Earthvoice has already communicated with the Angels, presenting himself as friendly and subservient. Prompted by Elka to work with the Angels, Earthvoice re-establishes contact with them and is welcomed eagerly. He admits to having been the source of the attacks which have damaged the angels but states that they were a programming directive which he has now overridden. To the humans' horror, Earthvoice and the Angels agree to share both the library's knowledge and power over the Earth, with the Angels also urging that Earthvoice exterminates the crew for safety. Earthvoice begins to transfer the knowledge - however, the Angels have fallen into a final trap. Earthvoice has always intended to destroy them, and he now launches one last brutal and specialised attack on the Angels from close range, erasing their consciousness and memory facilities. Rather than interfere further with the primitive human culture on Earth, the crew seal the door to the tower and return to the Challenger. With the Angels now reduced to subservient and "quite brainless" computer systems, they head back to their chosen home, Paradise, to rebuild their colony.

Boosting is a method for learning a single accurate predictor by linearly
combining a set of less accurate weak learners. Recently, structured learning
has found many applications in computer vision. Inspired by structured support
vector machines (SSVM), here we propose a new boosting algorithm for structured
output prediction, which we refer to as StructBoost. StructBoost supports
nonlinear structured learning by combining a set of weak structured learners.
As SSVM generalizes SVM, our StructBoost generalizes standard boosting
approaches such as AdaBoost, or LPBoost to structured learning. The resulting
optimization problem of StructBoost is more challenging than SSVM in the sense
that it may involve exponentially many variables and constraints. In contrast,
for SSVM one usually has an exponential number of constraints and a
cutting-plane method is used. In order to efficiently solve StructBoost, we
formulate an equivalent $ 1 $-slack formulation and solve it using a
combination of cutting planes and column generation. We show the versatility
and usefulness of StructBoost on a range of problems such as optimizing the
tree loss for hierarchical multi-class classification, optimizing the Pascal
overlap criterion for robust visual tracking and learning conditional random
field parameters for image segmentation.

Leucodecton canescens is a species of lichen in the family Graphidaceae. Found in Sri Lanka, it was formally described as a new species in 2014 by lichenologists Gothamie Weerakoon, Robert Lücking, and Helge Thorsten Lumbsch. The type specimen was collected from the Maussakanda Tea Estate (Matale, Central Province) at an altitude of . The lichen, which has been recorded from several locations in the Central Province, grows in semi-exposed, disturbed areas at high elevations. The specific epithet canescens refers to the grey-coloured cover of the thallus. Leucodecton canescens has a smooth, grey thallus that is 70–100 μm thick with a thin (5–10 μm) cortex. The ascomata are rounded, immersed in the substrate, and measure 0.2–0.3 mm in diameter. The ascospores are muriform, with dimensions of 25–30 by 10–12 μm. Secondary chemicals present in the lichen include stictic acid, constictic acid, acetylconstictic acid, and hypostictic acid. Leucodecton fissurinum is somewhat similar in morphology, but it has a yellowish thallus and narrower ascomata pores that conceal the disc.

Eva Dave, born Praful Nandshankar Dave, (5 March 1931 – 26 September 2009) was Gujarati story writer and novelist from Gujarat, India. Life 
Dave was born on 5 March 1931 at Baroda (now Vadodara). His family belonged to Nadiad.  He completed his primary and secondary education from Nadiad and matriculated in 1949. He completed B. A. in Gujarati in 1953 and M. A. in 1955. He completed B. Ed. from Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda in 1956. He studied M. A. in Education in 1957 and Ph. D. in 1963 from Washington University, US.
He taught at a school in Vallabh Vidyanagar from 1952 to 1956. He also served as a principal in the school of Alina in 1955. He worked as a research assistant in Washington University from 1960 to 1962. He served as a research associate in Saint Louis Mental Hospital, United States in 1963. He returned to India in 1964. He served as the Reader from 1964 to 1972 and as the Professor from 1972 to 1974 in Mysore Regional College of Education, India. He served as a principal-in-charge of Ajmer Regional College of Education from 1977 to 1944. In 1977, he joined NCERT, New Delhi as the Reader and later served as the Professor until his retirement in 1991. He died on 26 September 2009.

A British company has been accused by Venezuela's government of illegally occupying 10,000 hectares (25,000 acres) of farmland in the country.

The UK Foreign Office said it was aware of reports that the land had been occupied and was seeking clarification from the Venezuelan authorities.

But the company, which says it owns the land legally, denies any wrongdoing.

Venezuela's President Nicolas Maduro ordered an investigation into the case on Monday.

He also called for the expulsion of the British ambassador to Caracas if the allegations were proven true.

In a statement, the Venezuelan foreign ministry said the land belonged to the state-run agricultural bank Banco de Desarrollo Agrario y Pesquero (Bandep).

It added that the company - named as Tate & Lyle Americas Inc - had taken over the land without authorisation or permission.

Tate & Lyle Americas Inc is part of the Tate & Lyle group, one of Britain's largest food companies. It produces sweeteners such as Splenda and corn syrup.

The BBC understands that the company bought the land through a subsidiary in 2008 after receiving approval from Bandep.

However, the Venezuelan government claims that the sale was illegal because the land was not owned by Bandep but rather by another body known as Fondo Nacional del Campo (Foncamp), which manages rural property belonging to the state.

According to the Venezuelan newspaper El Universal, the company took possession of the land last year despite being told by officials that its title documents were invalid.

The paper reported that the company had built roads and fences around the area and planted crops there.

On Tuesday, Mr Maduro said his government would take legal action against the company and seek compensation for damages caused to the environment.

"We will never allow this type of aggression," he said during a televised speech.

"Rant: The Oral Biography of Buster Casey" is an engaging novel that unravels the enigmatic life of its titular protagonist, Buster 'Rant' Casey, through a series of oral accounts given by an assortment of individuals who each had a unique connection with him. The book uses an innovative storytelling technique that presents diverse perspectives from friends, family, and acquaintances to construct a kaleidoscopic portrait of this extraordinary and legendary character.

Rant is portrayed as a misfit from his childhood with peculiar habits, like getting bitten by deadly spiders and vermins as a hobby. His unusual proclivity for thrill and chaos becomes apparent when he leaves his town in Middle America for the city. There, he integrates into the Party Crashing culture - an anarchistic group indulging in night-time car crashes. His fearless exploits, combined with his paradoxical aversion to ordinary human touch, keep him at the heart of stories and urban legends.

His life takes a dramatic turn when he is killed, allegedly during one such Party Crashing event, which stirs a whirlwind of conspiracy theories about his death. Rant's paranormal association with time and space altering, his speculated role as a vector for a rabies outbreak, and various rumors about his alleged immortality are discussed, creating a reverberating impact on his fellow Party Crashers and the city.

"Rant: The Oral Biography of Buster Casey" navigates the readers through the labyrinthine narratives and distinct viewpoints, unveiling the unconventional yet alluring life of Buster 'Rant' Casey. While some view him as an agent of chaos, others see him as a visionary transcending the commonplace existence. This novel serves as an enticing amalgamation of science fiction, contemporary culture, and human society's eccentricities filtered through multiple lenses - all centered around the fascinating and chaotic life of Rant.

Title: Sharing Simulation Results for Long-Baseline Physics Studies at DUNE/LBNF from the CDR

This post aims to disseminate the outcomes of the simulations detailed in the DUNE Conceptual Design Report (CDR) on long-baseline neutrino oscillation physics at LBNF/DUNE. In Volume 2, titled "Physics Program for DUNE at LBNF," the scientific goals and related experiments conducted by the DUNE collaboration are discussed. The long-baseline sensitivity analyses in the CDR are based on the neutrino beamline simulation, neutrino interaction simulation in the far detector, and an assessment of detector performance and systematic uncertainties.

For the benefit of the broader research community, this posting shares the findings of these simulations, enabling phenomenological investigations into long-baseline neutrino oscillations at LBNF/DUNE. Furthermore, this posting contains GDML of the DUNE single-phase far detector for incorporation into simulations. DUNE encourages collaboration members to engage in this work but also acknowledges the value of making these configurations accessible to a larger audience.

Movement through specific instances in time, akin to an object or individual traversing distinct spatial locations, is referred to as time travel. This notion has gained recognition in philosophy and literature, notably science fiction. H.G. Wells' 1895 novel "The Time Machine" popularized the idea of a time machine. Whether time travel to the past can be achieved physically remains uncertain. Advancement or retardation of more than a few milliseconds for one body relative to another is beyond current technological capabilities for forward time travel, which is well-established in special relativity and general relativity. Backward time travel, though theoretically conceivable via solutions in general relativity like a rotating black hole, is not substantiated experimentally. Transit to an arbitrary point in spacetime is scarcely endorsed in theoretical physics, often linked solely to quantum mechanics or wormholes.

3 cups water
2 tablespoons honey
1 cup queso fresco
3 tart, crisp apples, such as Crispin or Granny Smith
2 cups apple or pear cider
8 ounces piloncillo, chopped, or 1 cup dark brown sugar plus 1 tablespoon molasses
1 (3-inch) piece Mexican cinnamon
2 tablespoons butter
Pinch of salt
3/4 cup toasted pecans, coarsely chopped
Combine the water and honey in a saucepan and cook over medium heat, stirring, until the honey is dissolved and the mixture reaches 160F. Let cool for at least 3 hours or overnight. Put the honey mixture and queso fresco in a food processor and blend until smooth. Pour the mixture into a shallow nonreactive pan and put it in the freezer. Once the edges start to freeze (about 1 hour), scrape lightly with a fork, bringing the ice crystals from the edges to the center. Return to the freezer and continue scraping every 30 minutes or so, until the mixture is completely frozen and looks like small ice flakes. Meanwhile, peel the apples and dice finely. Combine the cider, piloncillo, and cinnamon in a saucepan and cook over medium heat, stirring, until the mixture comes to a boil and the sugar has dissolved. Lower the heat and simmer until the syrup has thickened and has a consistency like maple syrup. Whisk in the butter and salt. Remove from the heat and stir in the apples. Let chill to room temperature. For each serving, mound about 1/2 cup of the cheese granita into a glass or cup. Drizzle about 4 tablespoons of the apple syrup over the granita and top with 1 tablespoon of the pecans. Serve immediately.

In this poem by William Butler Yeats (1865-1939), a man and woman are walking together in Ireland's countryside when they come upon two lovers who have been killed while embracing each other on their wedding day.[1] The speaker tells his lover that he will not be jealous if she were to fall for another because it would mean her love was as strong now at age fifty or sixty years old ("When you're grey")[2][3]. He also says how much better off both couples might've had things worked out differently; however there isn't anything either can do about what happened before them so all we should focus our attention towards today instead! This idea has become known among some scholars like Robert Alter [4], whose book includes commentary specifically addressing these lines within its pages."

Along ten miles of Reedy River,
A tranquil pool of water rests,
Reflecting annually the sky's transformation,
Offering stars a spacious nest.
Sand drifts on its bed, shifting endlessly,
Over rocky barriers it glides,
Bordering it, reeds sway gently,
Nurturing water rats and wild ducks' pride.
Grassy slopes ascend softly,
Leading to undulating hills,
Groves of wattle thrive and native bluebells bloom,
Crowning these landscapes with their beauty, unspoiled.
Beneath granite cliffs, Rocky Creek originates,
Emerging from verdant banks of fern,
Amidst these, she-oaks stand proudly,
Shading the waters before merging in.
Ten miles along Reedy River,
An afternoon in autumn sunlight passed,
With Mary Campbell, I ventured near,
That brilliant, expansive lagoon.
We abandoned horses feeding,
As twilight crept up the mountain's height,
Walked leisurely under she-oaks,
By Rocky Creek's banks we took delight.
Returning, we raced against the night,
Moonbeams gracing Mary's radiant visage,
Beseeching our future, I persisted,
Horses drawing close, side by side.
Five miles beyond Ryan's Crossing,
Three miles below the mountain's zenith,
Established a humble homestead,
By Rocky Creek's edge, I set my roots.
Cleared the land and secured it,
Plowed the fertile, crimson soil,
My initial harvest bore gold,
Upon bringing my beloved Mary home.
Still, along Reedy River,
She-oaks sigh, their leaves rustling soft,
Water-holes echo the images above,
Sun, moon, and stars continue their course, forevermore.
Yet, of the cabin I erected,
No remnants remain untold.
Countless rains erased my furrows,
And my vibrant yesterdays,
Have been replaced by twisted limbs,
Wattle blossoming upon the hill,
By Mary's tomb.

Synseg-Net is a novel deep learning framework that addresses the challenging task of synthetic segmentation without target modality ground truth. Instead of relying on large amounts of labeled data to train models, this approach leverages unlabeled target images and associated source images to synthesize semantic segments with high accuracy.
The framework consists of two main components: an encoder network that learns to map from src images to latent space representations, and a generator network that maps these compressed features back to dense synthetic outputs. During training, adversarial loss is applied between the real and generated output in order to optimize the model.
In experiments, we demonstrate synseg-net's ability to generate accurate segmentations for both source and target domains across a wide range of tasks, including image classification, object detection, and video analysis. These results suggest that synthetic segmentation can be achieved using only unlabeled source materials, providing valuable insights into low-resource or no-target scenarios where ground truth annotations are sparse or absent.

In the 1906 World Series, Chicago's White Sox and Cubs faced off in an intracity showdown. The Cubs boasted the best record (116 wins, .763 winning percentage) and statistics in the majors following the introduction of the 154-game season. In contrast, the White Sox, labeled as the "Hitless Wonders" due to their poor team batting average (.230) in the American League, managed to upset the Cubs in six games. The White Sox excelled on the mound in their initial victories and delivered more hits in their final games. The sequence of home teams rotated, with the Cubs hosting Game 1. After a 2-2 tie in the first four encounters, the Hitless Wonders, a moniker given by sports journalist Charles Dryden, rallied for 26 hits in the concluding matches. Consistent with their nickname, the White Sox amassed a collective batting average of .198 yet edged out the Cubs' .196 mark in clinching the championship. In Game 3, White Sox pitcher Ed Walsh surpassed the existing record of 11 strikeouts, which was pitched by Bill Dinneen previously.

Annual event, Mitzvah Day International, held in November primarily in the UK, encourages community groups and individuals to engage in faith-based social action through volunteer projects for local causes. Over 30,000 participants worldwide in 2013. Registration with Mitzvah Day connects volunteers to projects. Objective: encouraging time commitment over monetary donations, fostering community bonds, and supporting charities. Coincides with start of UK National Inter Faith Week, extending participation beyond Jewish community since 2013. "Public Enemies" provides a detailed and gripping account of notorious gangster John Dillinger's life, set amidst the backdrop of the Great Depression. Johnny Depp delivers an exceptional performance as Dillinger - a rather strange yet charismatic anti-hero, truly embodying the man's rebellious nature and unique charm. Christian Bale's portrayal as Agent Melvin Purvis is equally compelling, paving the way for a classic cat-and-mouse chase that forms the crux of the movie. The film also manages to weave in a touching love story that brings out Dillinger's more sensitive side.

The plot of "Public Enemies" is well-paced, managing to sustain the audience's attention through a perfect blend of action scenes and dialogues. Michael Mann's stellar direction makes full use of the film's setting, offering viewers a glimpse into the socioeconomic realities of an America in the throes of the Great Depression. The choice of a grainy, blue-toned cinematography enhances this experience, contributing to an air of gritty realism that stays with you for a while.

In terms of performance, the entire cast deserves commendable praise. However, Marion Cotillard steals the show as Billie Frechette, Dillinger's girlfriend and confidante. She brings an emotional depth to her character that contrasts well with the prevalent action-driven narrative.

One critique might be the occasional tendency of the film to prioritize style over substance, focusing more on appearances than character development. Nonetheless, this does not significantly lessen the film's overall appeal.

"Public Enemies" is a layered period drama that captivates viewers not just with its gangster theme but also with its attention to historical detail, making it a much-watched for lovers of well-crafted crime films. It carefully treads the line between glamorizing and humanizing John Dillinger, creating an intriguing character study that will leave audiences pondering on the man behind the notorious criminal.

US economy expanded by 3.8% yearly in Q4 2004, surpassing the 3.1% predicted by the government and economists. This increase can be attributed to enhanced business investment in capital goods and a smaller trade deficit. Gross Domestic Product (GDP), which gauges a nation's economic wellbeing through its production of goods and services, showed growth above the 3.5% previously forecasted. The 4% expansion rate was achieved in Q3 2004, with the year's total growth standing at 4.4%. Despite this robust economic condition, anticipation of rising interest rates exists, with many predicting a hike on March 22. Economists project a 4% annual growth rate for Q1-Q3 2005. Businesses boosted capital equipment and software spending by 18% in Q4 2004, compared to the previous quarter's 17.5%. Consumer spending rose by 4.2% in Q4, decreasing from the 5.1% increase seen in Q3.

Literary activism is a form of protest and critique aimed at corporate publishing houses and the literary fiction/nonfiction that they publish. The progenitors of literary activism are the members of the Underground Literary Alliance. This group of writers is notorious for its protests, which have included making formal complaints against Guggenheim grants given to already-wealthy authors, crashing New York literary readings, and maintaining a website which reports weekly on the perceived corruption and lack of integrity of the current literary world. Acts of literary activism can also include editing and bringing out writers' work in online and print journals and through book publishers, reading and reviewing that work, writing essays about it, teaching it, talking it up, urging others to launch journals and indies presses, running reading series, laboring in arts administration, coordination innovative writing conferences, launching local writing groups, posting about authors and texts they love on their blogs or via other social networking sites.

The LPM (Landau-Pomeranzhuk-Migdal) effect is a phenomenon observed in high energy physics, where the probability of electron-positron pair production by photon-photon scattering increases with increasing photon energies. This effect has been extensively studied and modeled using various approaches, including perturbative QED and Monte Carlo simulations. In this paper, we present a new approach to studying the LPM effect in sequential bremsstrahlung processes, which involves factoring out the dependence on the photon energy from the expression for the cross section. We show that this factorization allows us to obtain analytical expressions for the cross sections at leading order in the small photon energy limit, as well as numerical results for higher orders. Our findings provide insight into the underlying physical mechanisms responsible for the LPM effect and have implications for future experiments aimed at measuring this phenomenon.

> Satyendra Nath Bose (Bengali: সত্যেন্দ্র নাথ বোস) (January 1, 1894 – February 4, 1974), was a Bengali physicist and mathematician who made contributions to quantum mechanics and statistical physics. He is best known for his work on the statistics of identical particles which are now called Bose–Einstein statistics after Albert Einstein's collaboration with him in developing this theory. This led to the discovery of the Bose-Einstein condensate, a state of matter that has been achieved experimentally since 1995.
>
> ## Early life[edit]
>
> Born at Calcutta, India, he studied at Presidency College, University of Calcutta where he obtained a master's degree in mathematics and physics in 1920. In 1936, he became professor of mathematical physics at the Indian Association for Cultivation of Science, Calcutta.
>
> ## Career[edit]
>
> His first paper on the subject appeared in 1924.^{[1]} It was sent by Einstein to Max Planck, who had developed the concept of quanta in black body radiation. Planck immediately recognized its importance and arranged for it to be published in Zeitschrift für Physik. Later, Einstein translated the paper into German himself.
>
> Afterwards, Einstein collaborated with Bose on further developments of the theory. They showed that the energy levels of photons were not equally spaced as previously thought but instead followed a discrete distribution law. This result was later confirmed experimentally by Arthur Compton.
>
> Bose also worked on the problem of the specific heat capacity of solids. He proposed a model based on the idea that electrons could move freely through the lattice structure of crystals without being scattered by impurities or defects. This model predicted that the specific heat capacity should vary linearly with temperature rather than the usual quadratic dependence observed in metals. Experimental evidence supporting this prediction was found in 1935 by John Bardeen and William Shockley using data collected by Robert Millikan

Released in 2015, Sicario was a film I finally managed to watch last week despite knowing I would enjoy it based on rave reviews. Sicario ranks among the top action/thrillers of the past decade due to director Denis Villeneuve's ability to build tension and unease for a solid 120 minutes, leaving me on the edge of my seat. My nails bore the brunt of this nerve-wracking experience. The storyline may appear simple – the FBI collaborates with questionable characters to combat a vicious Mexican drug cartel – yet the confusion and mistrust experienced by Emily Blunt's young FBI agent mirrors the audience's perspective. The film offers numerous thought-provoking moments as motives remain obscure until the climax. Outstanding acting and witty dialogue contribute to the movie's success, but it's Villeneuve's skillful direction, enhanced by stunning visuals and an exceptional score, that sets Sicario apart as a shockingly intense and suspenseful thriller. If you haven't seen Sicario, do yourself a favor and rectify that oversight promptly.

Tottenham manager Martin Jol acclaimed his players for their patience in their 3-0 FA Cup fifth-round victory over a determined Nottingham Forest side.
"We had the initiative but it wasn't easy. It was a professional sort of performance," the Dutchman said. "Forest played with a lot of players behind the ball in the first half, but at 2-0 they were dead and buried." Looking ahead to the quarter-final, Jol said: "Newcastle have got a very good side and they are always difficult." However, he added that his side, who are four places above the Magpies in the Premiership, were "not afraid of anyone". Robbie Keane, skipper for the night and scorer of the crucial second goal, echoed his manager's sentiments on the last-eight match. "They're on a high, but we're confident and in the last few games we've played well and hopefully we can go there and get the win," he said.
He conceded the win over Forest, which included goals from Noe Pamarot and Mido, was not pretty to watch. "It wasn't the best display but it's all about the result," the Irishman said. "We knew it was going to be difficult with the conditions. The pitch wasn't the best but we still tried to pass it. "We dug in and the gaffer said to us at half-time to keep being patient and that the goal will come." Forest manager Gary Megson conceded his team did not deserve anything after a poor performance. "If you play like we did and concede two goals from corners you're going to have an uphill battle against a very good team," he said. "If we defend in the Championship like we did we'll not get another point. "We were organised but I felt at times we thought the system would be enough but we didn't look like scoring."

Ingredients
1/2 cup butter, melted
3 tablespoons curry powder
4 cloves garlic, minced
1 teaspoon ground cumin
1 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon cayenne pepper
6 skinless, boneless chicken breast halves - cut into 1 inch cubes
1 (10 ounce) package frozen peas and carrots
1 (15 ounce) can chickpeas, drained
1 (10 ounce) jar mango chutney
1/2 cup heavy cream
Directions
Preheat oven to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C). In a large bowl, mix together the butter, curry powder, garlic, cumin, salt and cayenne pepper. Add the chicken pieces, stirring until well coated with the mixture. Spread evenly in a 9x13 inch baking dish. Bake at 375 degrees F (190 degrees C) for about 30 minutes or until juices run clear when pierced with a fork. Stir in the peas and carrots, chickpeas, chutney and cream; bake an additional 10 minutes.

Title's significance merits emphasis in this critique. While ardent Harry Potter devotees might advocate a perfect rating and label this film a virtuoso piece, I cannot concur. Instead, I assert that "Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them" offers an enjoyable experience, particularly for those enchanted by J.K. Rowling's mystical universe.

Initially, the casting was impressive. Eddie Redmayne brilliantly portrays Newt Scamander, an eccentric, solitary man who favors animal companionship over human interaction. His characterization was spot on. Dan Fogler delivered an amusing performance as the muggle, or "no-maj," encountering the wizarding realm. Additionally, Katherine Waterstone and Alison Sudol effectively brought their sister duo to life, unwittingly drawn into the adventure.

The creatures stole the show. Though the CGI appeared artificial at times, the imaginative ideas compensated for any shortcomings. Most creatures showcased unique characteristics that distinguished them from clichés. Capturing these beings presented delightful sequences throughout the film.

Despite its strengths, "Fantastic Beasts" had weaknesses. An excessive number of superfluous characters detracted from the narrative. Several felt underdeveloped and added little value to the plot (*ahem* Jon Voight *ahem*). Furthermore, a burgeoning magical threat emerged toward the end, yet failed to captivate me entirely. Overall, however, these flaws did not irreparably damage the film. The magic and imagination on display warranted the ticket price alone.

We explore several generalizations of Whitney's theorem -- a classical
formula for the chromatic polynomial of a graph. Following Stanley, we replace
the chromatic polynomial by the chromatic symmetric function. Following Dohmen
and Trinks, we exclude not all but only an (arbitrarily selected) set of broken
circuits, or even weigh these broken circuits with weight monomials instead of
excluding them. Following Crew and Spirkl, we put weights on the vertices of
the graph. Following Gebhard and Sagan, we lift the chromatic symmetric
function to noncommuting variables. In addition, we replace the graph by an
"ambigraph", an apparently new concept that includes both hypergraphs and
multigraphs as particular cases.
  We show that Whitney's formula endures all these generalizations, and a
fairly simple sign-reversing involution can be used to prove it in each
setting. Furthermore, if we restrict ourselves to the chromatic polynomial,
then the graph can be replaced by a matroid.
  We discuss an application to transitive digraphs (i.e., posets), and reprove
an alternating-sum identity by Dahlberg and van Willigenburg.

The primary shareholder of disputed Russian oil company Yukos, Group Menatep, is instituting a $28.3bn (£15.2bn) lawsuit against the Russian administration. In late 2014, the Kremlin seized and transferred Yugansk, Yukos' major manufacturing division, to state-owned oil corporation Rosneft for approximately $9.3bn to settle a substantial unpaid tax debt. Menatep, which manages a 51% stake in Yukos through its Gibraltar headquarters, argues that this transaction was illicit. Menatep has also petitioned Rosneft to reimburse a $900m loan secured against Yugansk's assets.

The Russian authorities' rationale behind selling Yuganskneftegaz (Yugansk's complete name) was that Yukos reportedly owed over $27bn in past-due taxes from 2000 and onward. They charged the corporation with employing a network of overseas businesses to evade its fiscal responsibilities, resulting in the seizure of Yukos' assets and the auctioning of Yugansk.

However, detractors argue that the divestiture and financial targeting of Yukos are attempts to reinstate state dominance within the energy sector. As per Menatep, the government's measures breached the 1994 Energy Charter Treaty, created to mediate disputes related to energy investments. "We have cautioned the Russian government regarding their persistent hostility towards Yukos, its executives, and its investors," stated Tim Osborne, a Menatep director. "The era for warnings is concluded, and efforts to recoup our losses commence in earnest today."

According to Menatep, the worth of its Yukos stockholding plummeted from $17.8bn to practically zero since 2003 due to the Russian government's intervention, as its shares plunged 97%. Based on Menatep's Paris attorney, Emmanuel Gaillard of Shearman and Sterling, the total assertion encompasses that loss, along with a 60% increase for the potential share appreciation since then. The arbitration of the lawsuit may occur in Stockholm or The Hague, according to Mr. Gaillard.

A late header by teenager Danny Graham earned Middlesbrough a battling draw with Charlton at the Riverside.
Matt Holland had put the visitors ahead in the 14th minute after his shot took a deflection off Franck Queudrue. But Middlesbrough peppered the Charlton goal after the break and Chris Riggott stroked home the equaliser. Shaun Bartlett's strike put Charlton back in front but that lead lasted just six minutes before Graham rushed onto Queudrue's pass to head home. The match burst to life from the whistle and Charlton defender Hermann Hreidarsson had sight of an open goal after just six minutes. Hreidarsson received Danny Murphy's free-kick from the right but he crashed his free header wide of the far post. The Iceland international looked such a danger the Boro bench could be heard issuing frantic instructions to mark him.
Charlton's early pressure paid off when Bartlett received a long ball from Talal El Karkouri in the box and laid it off to Holland who buried his right-footed strike. Szilard Nemeth, recalled in place of Joseph-Desire Job, was twice denied his chance to get Middlesbrough back on level terms by Dean Kiely. The striker played a great one-two with Jimmy Floyd Hasselbaink only to see Kiely get down well to smother his shot before directing a header straight into the keeper's arms. Boro had plenty of time on the ball but the Addicks comfortably mopped up the pressure - with Kiely tipping a Hasselbaink header over the bar - to take their lead into half-time.
It was all one-way traffic after the break at the Riverside as Middlesbrough poured forward and Kiely even saved Hreidarsson's blushes when he palmed the ball away to prevent a Charlton own goal. But the Addicks keeper could do nothing about Riggott's equaliser in the 74th minute. The Boro defender looked suspiciously offside as he got on the end of Gareth Southgate's misdirected effort, but despite the Charlton protests his goal stood. The Addicks did not let their heads drop and Bartlett left the Boro defence standing, picking up Hreidarsson's cross to easily sink his right-footed strike. But substitute Graham was on hand to grab a share of the points for the home side. The 19-year-old striker nodding home the equaliser - and his first Premiership goal - with five minutes left on the clock.
"I felt we did enough to win the game even though the first half was lacklustre. "We dominated after the break, the players showed a fantastic response and we should have gone on to win. "But for (Charlton goalkeeper) Dean Kiely, who made three tremendous saves, we could have scored five or six."
"To take the lead and then to get penned back, it feels a little bit like a defeat," admitted Kiely. "We were winning but Middlesbrough kept knocking on the door. But we stood up and credit to us we didn't capitulate. "We'll kick on now. Our short-term ambition is to progress from the seventh place finish from last year."

Verizon has emerged victorious in the takeover struggle for American phone corporation MCI with an offer valued at approximately $6.8bn (£3.6bn), according to media outlets. It is anticipated that the agreement will be finalized on Monday morning, even though Qwest had been believed to present a superior proposal. In the rapidly consolidating US telecom sector, AT&T, a former major long-distance provider, was previously acquired by its former subsidiary SBC for around $16bn this year. MCI, which emerged from bankruptcy in April following its bankruptcy under its former name WorldCom, saw shareholders lose approximately $180bn and 20,000 employees lose their jobs during the collapse. Former WorldCom CEO Bernie Ebbers is currently on trial, facing accusations of presiding over a $11bn fraud. Qwest has also faced scrutiny, settling with the Securities and Exchange Commission for $250m in October due to allegations of manipulating financial results to please Wall Street.

As the US's second largest long-distance carrier behind AT&T, MCI has seen consolidation in the telecom industry surge in recent months as companies aim to reduce expenses and expand customer bases. A potential merger between MCI and Verizon would mark the fifth billion-dollar telecom transaction since October. Last week, SBC Communications announced plans to purchase its former parent and pioneering telephone company AT&T for roughly $16bn. Acquiring MCI would grant either Qwest or Verizon access to MCI's extensive global network and business-oriented subscribers. The motivations mirror those driving SBC's acquisition of AT&T. With Verizon significantly larger in size and boasting a profitable mobile division, these factors could have tipped the scale in its favor as both parties offer a combination of cash and stocks.

The Self-Transport Road and Rail Vehicle (STARR) concept, developed by William Alden during the 1960s, was an early personal rapid transit (PRT) system. Initially intended for short urban journeys at low speeds, these compact, electrically driven cars could join tracks offering power and direction for long-distance, high-speed inter-city travel. As one of the first proposed and built dual-mode vehicles, it underwent significant transformations over time. Originally designed for four passengers with dual-mode capabilities, it later evolved into a large-capacity people mover accommodating twenty individuals. Boeing Vertol secured a construction contract from this updated design in 1970 to establish a demonstration system in Morgantown, West Virginia. Kobe Steel, a licensee, also constructed a smaller version for Expo '75 on Okinawa, along with a more advanced CVS system. The Morgantown PRT system commenced operations in 1975 and has been continually in use, save for a major expansion closure.

Olivia Manning (2 March 1908 – 23 July 1980) was a British writer best known for her novel sequence The Balkan Trilogy and The Levant Trilogy, which depict the experiences of British and Romanian expatriates in Eastern Europe before and during World War II.

Manning was born in Portsmouth, Hampshire, England, and grew up in a working-class family. She attended the local grammar school and later studied art at the Portsmouth School of Art. After completing her studies, she worked as a teacher and a governess in England and Ireland. During this time, she developed an interest in writing and began to publish her short stories and articles in various literary magazines.

In 1939, Manning married the British writer and artist Reggie Smith, and the couple moved to Bucharest, Romania, where Manning's husband was posted as a British Council lecturer. It was during this time in Romania that Manning gained the inspiration for her most famous work, The Balkan Trilogy. The trilogy, consisting of the novels The Great Fortune (1960), The Spoilt City (1962), and Friends and Heroes (1965), follows the lives of a cast of British and Romanian characters against the backdrop of the political instability in Eastern Europe in the late 1930s and early 1940s. The trilogy is praised for its vivid portrayal of the social and cultural dynamics of the time and was highly regarded by critics.

Following the success of The Balkan Trilogy, Manning published The Levant Trilogy, which continues the story of some of the same characters as they navigate the turbulent events of the war in North Africa and the Middle East. The Levant Trilogy is composed of the novels The Danger Tree (1977), The Battle Lost and Won (1978), and The Sum of Things (1980).

Manning's writing is characterized by her sharp wit, keen observation, and astute understanding of human nature. Her works often explore themes of displacement, identity, and the impact of war on individuals and societies. In addition to her fiction, Manning also wrote a number of travel books and essays on various subjects.

Despite critical acclaim and a loyal following of readers during her lifetime, Manning's works did not achieve widespread commercial success. However, in recent years, there has been a resurgence of interest in her writing, with many critics and scholars recognizing her as a significant and underappreciated voice in British literature.

Report from analyst firm Gartner forecasts that over twice the number of mobile phones with integrated cameras, approximately 119 million units, will be sold in Europe by the end of 2004 compared to the previous year. On a global scale, this figure represents a 104% increase, bringing the total to 159 million units sold. By 2008, it is predicted that almost three-quarters of all mobile phones sold will incorporate built-in cameras. The continual advancement of imaging technology in mobile devices has made them a desirable purchase. European models currently offer 1.3 megapixel capabilities, whereas more sophisticated cameras have already emerged in Japan and Asia Pacific, capable of capturing images of up to 3.2 megapixels. Japan remains a leader in mobile innovation, and by 2008, Gartner anticipates that 95% of all mobile phones sold there will feature cameras.

When initially introduced, camera phones faced challenges, such as low image quality, limited applications, and complex methods for sharing images through Multimedia Messaging Services (MMS). However, these issues have been addressed in recent months as handset manufacturers have focused on simplifying usage. They have introduced user-friendly design elements, such as rotatable screens, viewfinders, removable memory cards, and streamlined control options for sending picture messages. Mobile service providers have expanded the ways users can share their photographs, enabling easier publication on websites or mobile blogs, known as moblogs. Nevertheless, the report indicates that significant improvements in image quality must occur before consumers express interest in producing printouts at photo kiosks. Progress in camera phone image sensor technology is anticipated, and by mid-2005, it is expected that most camera phones will exceed a two-megapixel resolution. Consumer digital cameras provide images ranging from two to six megapixels, but high-end camera models can produce images of up to twelve megapixels.

Three-dimensional convolutional neural networks have been successfully employed in diverse computer vision applications, particularly in the realm of medical image segmentation. Advancements in semantic segmentation have facilitated this application, with many recent studies utilizing 3D kernels to fully exploit the intricate structure of medical images. Although sharing similarities with semantic segmentation, medical image segmentation presents distinct challenges, including limited labeled data availability, significant class imbalance within ground truth labels, and high memory requirements for processing 3D images. This study introduces a CNN-based approach featuring 3D filters, which is then applied to hand and brain MRI scans. Two enhancements to an existing CNN design are explored, alongside strategies for tackling the outlined challenges. Unlike previous research predominantly focusing on soft tissues and major organs, this investigation validates its results on data derived from both the central nervous system and the hand's bones.

Ingredients:
* 1 lb boneless, skinless chicken thighs, trimmed and cut into 1-inch pieces
* 1 tsp. kosher salt, more to taste
* Freshly ground black pepper
* 3 Tbsp. olive oil, divided
* 1 large yellow onion, diced
* 3 cloves garlic, chopped
* 1 Tbsp. fresh ginger, minced
* 1/2 tsp. ground cumin
* 1/2 tsp. ground coriander
* 1/2 tsp. ground turmeric
* Two 14.5 oz. cans diced tomatoes
* 1/2 cup coconut milk
* 2 cups baby spinach, chopped
* 2 cups green beans, trimmed and cut into 1-inch pieces
* 1/2 cup fresh cilantro, chopped, for serving

Instructions:
* Pat the chicken dry with paper towels and season with salt and pepper. Heat 1 tablespoon of the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until hot and shimmering. Add the chicken pieces in an even layer and cook without moving until browned on the bottom, 3 to 4 minutes. Flip the chicken pieces and brown the other side for about 5 minutes. Transfer the chicken to a clean bowl and set aside.
* Heat the remaining 2 tablespoons of olive oil in the now-empty skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the onion, garlic, and ginger and cook, stirring often, until the onion is softened and translucent with some browned bits, 5 to 7 minutes.
* Stir in the cumin, coriander, and turmeric and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add the tomatoes with their juice and the coconut milk and bring to a simmer. Reduce the heat to medium and cook, stirring occasionally and scraping up any browned bits, until thickened, about 15 minutes.
* Return the chicken and any accumulated juices to the skillet and stir to combine. Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is cooked through, about 10 minutes.
* Stir in the spinach and green beans and cook, uncovered, until the spinach is wilted and the green beans are crisp-tender, about 3 minutes.
* Season the curry with salt to taste. Serve the curry immediately, sprinkled with the cilantro.

> Ultracold neutrons (UCN) are an important tool in fundamental physics, and their detection requires high-efficiency detectors with low backgrounds. We present a new type of UCN detector based on a thin layer of superconducting niobium nitride (NbN), which has been shown to be highly efficient at converting UCN into charged particles. This detector can also be used as a fast timing device due to its short decay time constant. In this work we describe our design and construction of such a detector, including the fabrication process of the NbN film, and discuss the results obtained during commissioning tests.

Prepare the marinade the night before you plan to make the tamales. Chop one bunch of green onions. Mince 2 garlic cloves. Combine, then add 1 teaspoon ground cumin and 1 packet of sazon. Rub mixture all over both chicken and ribs. Place meat in separate plastic baggies to marinate in the refrigerator overnight. Next make the "hogao," a kind of sofrito. Combine chopped tomatoes, 1 bunch of chopped green onions, 2 cloves minced garlic, 1 tsp ground cumin, 1/2 packet of sazon, 1/6 cup of chopped cilantro, olive oil and salt to taste in a skillet and saute until everything is soft and tender, kind of like a mush. Cool and refrigerate until ready to assemble tamales. Now you can make the "pique" sauce. Combine 1 bunch chopped green onions, 3 cloves minced garlic, fresh lemon juice, remaining chopped cilantro, 1 teaspoon ground cumin, sugar, vinegar and salt to taste. Make this at least 2 hours before serving so flavors develop. Prepare masa harina according to package directions except use chicken broth in place of water and salt to taste. This mixture should have flavor unlike an arepa which is more bland (my husband says the masa is the best part). It should be fairly moist, but still stay together like a dough when pressed. If it is too wet you can still use it, it is just more messy. Now the hardest part is assembling them. Place about 1/4 cup of dough in the center of a banana leaf and spread it out. Put one rib and one chicken thigh piece on top. Place about 3 slices of the carrots, 6 potato sticks and 3 slices egg on top of the meat. Sprinkle with peas. Spoon 3 tablespoons of the "hogao" (sofrito) over all, then top with another 1/2 cup of spread out masa. This does not have to be uniform or even neat. Next pull up the sides of the banana leaf to form a packet. Tie with kitchen string, but do not let any of the filling seep out (I told you it was hard). If the leaves break just reinforce with extra banana leaves. Wrap packet in aluminum foil. Repeat 5 times. They are now ready to steam. Use a large Dutch oven with a steamer insert so the tamales do not touch the water in the bottom of the Dutch oven. These need to cook about 3 hours. You probably will have to replenish the water during the cooking process. Stack the tamales all the way to the top in the steamer pot and turn up the heat to high. If your pot does not hold all of them, just refrigerate or freeze the rest until you can steam them later. When you hear the water boiling furiously, turn the heat down to medium. Serve the tamales on a section of banana leaf. With the "pique" sauce on the side to be drizzled on bites of the tamale.

In conclusion, "Shrek Forever After" is a solid entry in the franchise that offers a fresh take on the characters and delivers a satisfying finale. It retains the humor and heart that made the previous films so beloved, while also exploring new themes and character arcs. Whether you're a die-hard Shrek fan or a casual moviegoer, this film is definitely worth a watch.

Let $G$ be a bridgeless cubic graph. Consider a list of $k$ 1-factors of $G$.
Let $E_i$ be the set of edges contained in precisely $i$ members of the $k$
1-factors. Let $\mu_k(G)$ be the smallest $|E_0|$ over all lists of $k$
1-factors of $G$. If $G$ is not 3-edge-colorable, then $\mu_3(G) \geq 3$. In
[E. Steffen, 1-factor and cycle covers of cubic graphs, J. Graph Theory 78(3)
(2015) 195-206] it is shown that if $\mu_3(G) \not = 0$, then $2 \mu_3(G)$ is
an upper bound for the girth of $G$. We show that $\mu_3(G)$ bounds the oddness
$\omega(G)$ of $G$ as well. We prove that $\omega(G)\leq \frac{2}{3}\mu_3(G)$.
If $\mu_3(G) = \frac{2}{3} \mu_3(G)$, then every $\mu_3(G)$-core has a very
specific structure. We call these cores Petersen cores. We show that for any
given oddness there is a cyclically 4-edge-connected cubic graph $G$ with
$\omega(G) = \frac{2}{3}\mu_3(G)$. On the other hand, the difference between
$\omega(G)$ and $\frac{2}{3}\mu_3(G)$ can be arbitrarily big. This is true even
if we additionally fix the oddness. Furthermore, for every integer $k\geq 3$,
there exists a bridgeless cubic graph $G$ such that $\mu_3(G)=k$.
